AI-01.1.summary: This 12-minute video shows how to write prompts that make an approved SCG GenAI copilot useful for analysis rather than generic text, using a role–context–data–task–format structure. It matters because most weak copilot output at SCG comes from thin prompts, not weak tools, and because prompts must respect SCG data classification rules.
objectives: You can write an analysis prompt with role, context, data, task and output format specified.
You can decide what plant, customer or cost data may be pasted into an approved tool under SCG data classification.
keyPoints: Use the five-part pattern: role, business context, the data itself, the specific analytical task, and the output format you want.
Paste the data into the prompt; do not ask the tool to recall SCG figures it cannot see.
Only approved internal tools, and only data classified Internal or below — no customer contracts, personal data or unreleased financials.
Ask for the reasoning steps and assumptions, not just the answer, so the output can be checked.
Iterate: a second prompt that says what was wrong with the first output is usually faster than rewriting from scratch.
AI-01.1.scgExample: A logistics supervisor at a Saraburi cement plant has 12 weeks of dispatch data showing truck turnaround rising from 47 to 63 minutes. She prompts: "You are a logistics analyst. Below is weekly truck turnaround time and daily dispatch volume for our bagged cement yard. Identify which weeks broke trend, state the correlation with volume, and list three possible causes I should check in the yard. Output: table plus three bullets, flag assumptions." The copilot flags weeks 9–12 and notes turnaround rose faster than volume, suggesting a process rather than capacity issue. She then checks the weighbridge queue log and finds a second shift handover gap.
AI-01.1.practiceTask: Take one real data extract you already own (20–60 rows: downtime, complaints, overtime, dealer orders). Write one prompt using all five parts, run it in the approved tool, then write a second refining prompt. Output: a one-page note with prompt v1, prompt v2, and two sentences on what improved.
commonMistakes: Asking a general question ("how do we improve turnaround?") with no data attached, producing textbook advice.
Pasting confidential or personal data because the tool is internal — classification rules still apply.
Accepting the first output as final instead of refining with a follow-up prompt.

quickCheck.question: Which prompt is most likely to produce usable analysis?
options: "Analyse our packaging plant performance."

"You are a production analyst. Here are 12 weeks of line OEE and changeover counts [data]. Identify the three weeks with the largest OEE drop and state likely drivers. Output: table plus assumptions."
"What is OEE and how is it calculated?"
"Give me best practices for packaging productivity in Southeast Asia."
quickCheck.why: It supplies role, context, actual data, a specific task and an output format — the five-part pattern.

quickCheck.question: A supervisor wants to analyse a customer's unsigned pricing agreement using the copilot. What should she do?
options: Paste it in; the tool is SCG-approved
Summarise it in her own words and paste that
Check data classification first and use the approved handling route for confidential documents
Remove the customer name and paste the rest
quickCheck.why: Tool approval does not override data classification; confidential commercial documents need the approved handling route.

quickCheck.question: The first output misses a key constraint. What is the fastest fix?
options: Start a new chat with a longer prompt
Tell the copilot what was wrong and what constraint to apply, then re-run
Do the analysis manually
Ask a colleague to try the same prompt
quickCheck.why: Iterative correction within the same context is normally faster and preserves the data already supplied.

AI-01.1.coachPrompt: Show me a prompt you used this week on real work data — which part of the five-part pattern did you have to add before the output became usable?

AI-01.2.summary: An 18-minute reading on using a copilot to move from raw thinking to a structured internal proposal — capex request, process change, supplier switch — while keeping the argument and numbers your own. It matters because proposals are where poor AI use is most visible: fluent text that a committee can puncture in two questions.
objectives: You can brief a copilot with the decision, audience, constraints and evidence so it drafts a structured proposal skeleton.
You can identify which parts of a proposal must never be AI-generated and rewrite them yourself.
keyPoints: Brief before you draft: state the ask, the approver, the budget or policy constraints, and the three to five facts that carry the argument.
Ask for structure first (headings and the one-line claim under each), then expand section by section — one long prompt gives generic prose.
Numbers, assumptions, risks and commitments are yours; the copilot may format them but must not invent them.
Force the counter-case: ask the copilot to list the five questions a sceptical approver would ask, then answer them in the draft.
Cut AI padding — hedging phrases, repeated benefit claims and adjectives. SCG committees read for the number and the risk.
AI-01.2.scgExample: A chemicals maintenance manager needs THB 2.8m to replace two aging pumps. He briefs the copilot with the ask, the approver (plant capex committee), last year's 4 unplanned stoppages costing about THB 1.1m, and the vendor quote validity date. He asks for a four-section skeleton plus the eight toughest committee questions; the copilot asks why refurbishment was ruled out — which he had not addressed. He adds a half-page refurbishment comparison and the proposal passes at first review.
AI-01.2.practiceTask: Pick a proposal you owe someone in the next month. Spend 10 minutes writing the brief (ask, approver, constraints, key facts), then use the copilot to generate a skeleton and the sceptic's questions. Output: a one-page skeleton with your own numbers inserted and at least two objections you had not previously planned to answer.
commonMistakes: Letting the copilot supply plausible-sounding figures or payback periods that were never in your brief.
Sending polished AI prose that reads fluently but contains no owner, no date and no decision being requested.
Skipping the counter-case step, so the proposal is only tested for the first time in the committee room.

quickCheck.question: Which element must come from the author, not the copilot?
options: Section headings
The payback calculation and its assumptions
Grammar and tone
Summary of a policy you pasted in
quickCheck.why: Numbers and assumptions carry accountability; the copilot has no source for them unless you supply it.

quickCheck.question: Why ask for the skeleton before the full draft?
options: It uses fewer tokens
It lets you correct the argument structure before investing in prose
It is a compliance requirement
It makes the text shorter
quickCheck.why: Fixing the logic at skeleton stage is far cheaper than rewriting a finished draft.

quickCheck.question: What is the main value of asking for "the questions a sceptical approver would ask"?
options: It flatters the approver
It surfaces gaps in the argument before submission
It shortens the proposal
It transfers accountability to the tool
quickCheck.why: The counter-case exposes unaddressed alternatives and risks while there is still time to close them.

AI-01.2.coachPrompt: In the proposal you drafted with the copilot, which sentences did you have to rewrite yourself and why?

AI-01.3.summary: A 25-minute exercise in verifying copilot output against the underlying source data before it reaches a decision. It matters because AI errors at SCG are usually quiet ones — a mis-added total, a dropped row, a confidently wrong cause — that survive until someone acts on them.
objectives: You can run a four-step verification (recompute, trace, scope, challenge) on an AI-produced analysis.
You can mark an output as verified, partially verified or unverified and say what evidence supports each claim.
keyPoints: Recompute at least one headline number by hand or in Excel; if it fails, treat the whole output as suspect.
Trace every claim back to a row, a document or a system report — a claim with no traceable source is a hypothesis, not a finding.
Check scope: did the tool use all the rows, the right date range, the right sites, the right units (tonnes vs bags, THB vs USD)?
Challenge causal language: copilots turn correlation into cause easily; demote "because" to "may be linked to" unless you have evidence.
Label the output before circulating: verified / partially verified / unverified, with initials and date.
AI-01.3.scgExample: A shared-services analyst asks the copilot to summarise 340 supplier invoice exceptions. The output says 62% of exceptions come from three vendors and cost THB 480k in late-payment interest. She recomputes: the 62% is right, but the THB 480k assumed all exceptions were paid late, whereas 90 were resolved within terms — the true figure is about THB 210k. She circulates the vendor concentration finding as verified and the cost figure, corrected, as partially verified with the assumption stated.
AI-01.3.practiceTask: Take an AI-generated analysis you produced in AI-01.1 or from recent work. Recompute one headline number, trace three claims to source, and check the scope of the data used. Output: the original output annotated with V / PV / U per claim, plus a short note of any error found and its size.
commonMistakes: Checking only whether the output sounds reasonable instead of recomputing a number.
Verifying the maths but not the scope — correct arithmetic on the wrong date range or the wrong plant.
Forwarding output without a verification label, so the next reader assumes someone else already checked it.

quickCheck.question: The copilot reports a total that is 3% off your recomputation. What is the right response?
options: Accept it; 3% is within tolerance
Correct the total and re-check the rest of the output, since the error source is unknown
Ignore the total and use the narrative
Re-run the same prompt and use whichever total appears twice
quickCheck.why: An unexplained arithmetic error means the underlying handling of the data is unreliable until you find the cause.

quickCheck.question: Which is a scope check rather than a maths check?
options: Re-adding the column
Confirming the extract covered all four plants and the full quarter
Checking the percentage denominators
Recalculating the average
quickCheck.why: Scope concerns which data was included, not whether the arithmetic on it was correct.

quickCheck.question: The output says "downtime rose because of the new shift pattern." You have no evidence beyond timing. What should you do?
options: Keep the wording; it is plausible
Rewrite as "downtime rose in the same period as the new shift pattern" and list it as a hypothesis to test
Delete the finding
Ask the copilot to confirm it
quickCheck.why: Coincidence in timing is correlation; causal wording must be demoted until evidence exists.

AI-01.3.coachPrompt: What error did your verification catch this month, and what would it have cost if it had reached the decision?

AI-02.1.summary: A 12-minute video on compressing a decision onto one page: the question, the options, the evidence, the risks and the recommendation. It matters because most delay at SCG comes from decisions that are never clearly stated, so meetings re-open the framing instead of choosing.
objectives: You can state a decision as a single closed question with a named decision-maker and a deadline.
You can lay out two to four genuine options with the evidence and trade-off for each on one page.
keyPoints: Write the question so it can be answered yes/no or by picking an option — "improve delivery" is a topic, not a decision.
Name the decision-maker, the date needed and what happens if no decision is made.
Offer at least two real options; "do nothing" is always one and must be costed.
Attach the two or three pieces of evidence that would change the answer, not everything you have.
State the recommendation and your confidence in it — the reader needs your judgement, not neutrality.
AI-02.1.scgExample: A packaging plant manager frames: "Should we move corrugator line 2 to a 3-shift pattern from 1 October? Decision: plant director, by 15 September; if no decision, we continue overtime at about THB 350k/month." Options: keep overtime, 3-shift, or outsource 15% of volume. Evidence: order book up 18% for Q4, current OEE 71%, and 6 of 9 operators willing to shift. Recommendation: 3-shift, medium confidence, contingent on the operator survey holding above 6.
AI-02.1.practiceTask: Take a decision currently stuck in your area. Write it on one page: question, decision-maker, deadline, cost of no decision, two to four options with one line of evidence each, and your recommendation with confidence. Output: the one-pager, sent to the decision-maker or your manager for reaction.
commonMistakes: Framing a topic or a problem statement instead of a closed question with a named owner.
Listing a preferred option plus two straw men, which forces the reader to re-do the analysis.
Omitting the cost of doing nothing, so delay looks free.

quickCheck.question: Which is a properly framed decision?
options: "Review dealer credit terms."
"Should we reduce standard dealer credit from 60 to 45 days for the Northeast region from Q1? Owner: commercial director, decide by 20 November."
"Dealer credit is too generous."
"How can we improve cash collection?"
quickCheck.why: It is closed, scoped, dated and has a named decision-maker.

quickCheck.question: Why must "do nothing" be costed?
options: To lengthen the paper
Because delay has a real cost and otherwise looks free
Because policy requires three options
To make the recommendation look better
quickCheck.why: Without a cost of inaction, the status quo is treated as the zero-risk baseline, which it rarely is.

quickCheck.question: How much evidence belongs on the one-pager?
options: Everything collected, as an appendix index
The two or three facts that would change the answer
Only financial data
Whatever the copilot produced
quickCheck.why: Decision-relevant evidence is what changes the choice; the rest is background.

AI-02.1.coachPrompt: Read me the decision question from your one-pager — can the owner answer it with a single choice today?

AI-02.2.summary: An 18-minute reading on judging how much weight different evidence deserves and pairing each option with its risks. It matters because SCG managers routinely mix strong system data with one loud customer complaint and treat both as equally decisive.
objectives: You can rank evidence by source quality, recency and relevance before using it in a decision.
You can attach likelihood, impact and an early-warning indicator to the main risk of each option.
keyPoints: Grade evidence: system-of-record data > structured sampling > a single report > recalled opinion. Say the grade out loud in the paper.
Check recency and scope — 2023 dealer data may not describe 2025 behaviour, and one plant does not describe four.
Separate what the data shows from what you infer; inferences need an explicit assumption statement.
For each option state the main risk, its rough likelihood and impact, and one mitigation you would actually fund.
Define an early-warning indicator and a review date so a wrong decision is caught in weeks, not quarters.
AI-02.2.scgExample: A regional sales manager weighs cutting a slow-moving mortar SKU. Evidence: two years of SAP sales history showing 0.4% of regional volume (strong), a warehouse survey of stock ageing (medium), and two dealers saying the SKU wins them projects (weak, unrepresentative, 2 of 140 dealers). He calls the dealers' claim a hypothesis and checks order lines: the SKU appears in 6% of orders from the top 20 dealers. He recommends delisting in all channels except the top-20 dealer list, with a review after two quarters and monthly order-line share as the early-warning indicator.
AI-02.2.practiceTask: Take the one-pager from AI-02.1. Grade each piece of evidence strong/medium/weak with one line of justification, then add a risk line per option with likelihood, impact, mitigation and an early-warning indicator. Output: the revised one-pager, plus a note of any option whose ranking changed after grading.
commonMistakes: Treating vivid anecdotes as equal to system data because they are recent and emotionally persuasive.
Listing risks with no likelihood, impact or mitigation, so they are acknowledged but not managed.
Using data that is accurate but out of scope — one plant, one region, one season — as if it were general.

quickCheck.question: Which evidence should normally carry most weight in a volume decision?
options: Two years of SAP shipment records
A senior manager's recollection of last year
Feedback from the two most vocal dealers
A competitor's press release
quickCheck.why: System-of-record data is the most complete and least biased of the four.

quickCheck.question: A risk is listed as "supply disruption possible." What is missing?
options: Nothing; the risk is identified
Likelihood, impact, mitigation and an early-warning indicator
A different risk category
Approval from procurement
quickCheck.why: A risk is only manageable once its size and the trigger to act on it are stated.

quickCheck.question: Why set a review date when recommending an option?
options: To satisfy audit
To catch a wrong decision early and correct it cheaply
To delay the decision
To share accountability
quickCheck.why: A review date converts an irreversible bet into a monitored one.

AI-02.2.coachPrompt: Which piece of evidence in your last decision turned out to be weaker than you first treated it, and how did you find out?

AI-02.3.summary: A 25-minute exercise in writing a decision record: what was decided, by whom, on what evidence, what was rejected and when it will be reviewed. It matters because SCG teams frequently re-litigate settled decisions or repeat failed ones when the reasoning was never written down.
objectives: You can write a decision record of under one page covering decision, owner, evidence, rejected options, assumptions and review date.
You can run a review against a past record and judge whether the decision or the assumptions were wrong.
keyPoints: Record six fields: decision, owner and date, options rejected and why, key evidence and its grade, assumptions, review date and trigger.
Write it within 48 hours, while the rejected options and their reasons are still fresh.
Record the assumptions explicitly — most decisions fail because an assumption broke, not because the logic was bad.
Store it where the next person will look: the project folder or the meeting minute, not a personal drive.
At review, separate a bad decision from a good decision with a bad outcome; only the first should change how you decide next time.
AI-02.3.scgExample: A shared-services team decides to keep manual three-way matching for one supplier group rather than automate it. The record states: owner, finance operations manager, 12 March; rejected full automation because only 140 invoices/month and the interface build was quoted at 3 months; assumption — volume stays below 200/month; review 30 September, triggered earlier if volume exceeds 200. In August volume hits 260 after a sourcing change; the trigger fires, and the team reopens automation with four months saved because the assumption was written down.
AI-02.3.practiceTask: Write a decision record for one decision you made in the last month using the six fields, and open one record (yours or your team's) from six or more months ago and assess whether its assumptions still hold. Output: one new record plus a three-line review verdict — assumptions hold / broken / decision was flawed.
commonMistakes: Recording only the chosen option, so future readers cannot see what was already ruled out and why.
Leaving assumptions implicit, which makes it impossible to know when the decision should be revisited.
Treating any bad outcome as a bad decision, which pushes teams towards over-caution rather than better reasoning.

quickCheck.question: Which field is most often omitted and most costly to omit?
options: The date
The assumptions and review trigger
The document title
The attendee list
quickCheck.why: Without stated assumptions and a trigger, nobody knows when conditions have changed enough to revisit.

quickCheck.question: An option was rejected in March. It resurfaces in July. What should happen?
options: Re-analyse from scratch
Check the record for why it was rejected and whether those reasons still hold
Escalate to the director
Accept it, since circumstances always change
quickCheck.why: The record turns a full re-analysis into a short test of whether the original reasons still apply.

quickCheck.question: A well-reasoned decision produced a poor result due to an unforeseeable supplier failure. How should the review classify it?
options: Bad decision; change the process
Good decision, bad outcome; note the new risk for future records
No review needed
Blame the evidence grading
quickCheck.why: Judging decisions only by outcomes rewards luck and drives excessive caution; the learning here is the new risk.

AI-02.3.coachPrompt: Open one decision record you wrote — which assumption in it is closest to breaking right now?

OPEX-01.1.summary: This 12-minute video shows how to turn a raw operations spreadsheet into a three-part improvement narrative: what is happening, why it matters in money or risk, and what decision you need. At SCG, most improvement proposals die because the data is presented as a table dump rather than as a story a plant manager or business head can act on in two minutes.
objectives: You can state the situation–complication–ask structure of an improvement story in your own words
You can convert one of your routine reports into a single headline sentence with a number attached
You can identify which rows and columns in a spreadsheet are noise for a given audience
keyPoints: Start from the decision you want, not from the data you have; the ask defines what evidence is relevant.
Use one headline sentence per slide: subject, movement, number, period (e.g. 'Kiln 3 unplanned stops rose 40% in Q2').
Translate technical units into business units at least once: tonnes lost, THB, hours of crew time, customer complaints.
Show the comparison, not just the level — versus last period, versus target, versus best-performing line or plant.
Keep the raw spreadsheet as an appendix; the story slide should survive being read without you in the room.
OPEX-01.1.scgExample: A packaging plant supervisor in Rayong had a 14-tab spreadsheet of corrugator downtime. She rebuilt it into one line: 'Corrugator 2 lost 118 hours in Q2, 62% from splice failures, worth about THB 3.1 million in conversion margin.' The second slide showed splice failures by shift, revealing night shift at 3x the day rate. The ask was one sentence: approve a 6-week night-shift splice coaching trial at THB 180,000.
OPEX-01.1.practiceTask: Take one report you already send weekly. Write, on a single page: (1) one headline sentence with a number and a period, (2) two supporting facts, (3) one specific ask with a cost or resource figure. Delete every number that does not serve those three items. Expected output: a one-page story draft plus a note of how many numbers you removed.
commonMistakes: Opening with methodology and data sources before the audience knows why they should care.
Presenting absolute values with no comparison, so the audience cannot tell if the number is good or bad.
Ending with 'for your information' instead of a specific decision or resource request.

quickCheck.question: What should determine which data goes into your improvement story?
options: The data that was easiest to extract
The decision you are asking the audience to make
Everything available, so nobody can challenge you
The format the previous report used
quickCheck.why: The ask defines relevance; evidence is selected to support a decision, not to demonstrate effort.

quickCheck.question: Which headline is strongest for a plant leadership review?
options: Downtime analysis Q2 2027
Kiln 3 unplanned stops rose 40% versus Q1, costing THB 4.2m
We have collected downtime data from four sources
Downtime remains an area of focus
quickCheck.why: It names the subject, the movement, the comparison period and the business value.

quickCheck.question: Why translate technical units into THB or hours at least once?
options: Finance requires it in all reports
It makes the slide look more professional
It lets non-specialist decision makers compare this issue against other calls on their budget
It removes the need for technical detail
quickCheck.why: A common unit allows leaders to prioritise across unrelated problems.

OPEX-01.1.coachPrompt: Show me the last report you sent — what single sentence would you now lead with, and what decision were you actually asking for?

OPEX-01.2.summary: This reading maps the small set of charts that cover almost all OpEx situations — trend, comparison, distribution, contribution and correlation — and gives rules for choosing between them. Poor chart choice is the most common reason SCG improvement data is misread in reviews, leading to arguments about the picture rather than the problem.
objectives: You can match a chart type to the question being asked about your data
You can redesign a cluttered chart so the main message is visible in five seconds
You can explain why pie charts and dual axes are usually poor choices in OpEx reporting
keyPoints: Question first: 'how is it changing?' = line; 'who is bigger?' = horizontal bar; 'what makes up the total?' = stacked bar or Pareto; 'is there a relationship?' = scatter.
A Pareto chart is the default for defect, downtime and complaint causes because it shows both size and priority.
A run chart with the mean and target lines beats a table for showing whether a change actually held.
Avoid pie charts beyond three slices, dual y-axes, and 3D effects — they invite misreading of relative size.
Pre-attentive cues do the work: grey out everything except the one bar or line you want discussed, and put the message in the chart title.
OPEX-01.2.scgExample: A cement logistics team reported truck turnaround time as a table of 26 depots. Rearranged as a horizontal bar chart sorted descending, with the six depots above the 90-minute standard coloured orange and the rest grey, the discussion moved in one minute to Saraburi and Khon Kaen. A second run chart of Saraburi's weekly average, with the target line at 90 minutes, showed the drift began in week 9 — the week a weighbridge was taken offline.
OPEX-01.2.practiceTask: Pick three charts from your latest function pack. For each, write the one question it should answer, judge whether the chart type fits, and rebuild the worst one. Apply: sort the data, grey out non-focus series, and rewrite the title as a sentence stating the message. Expected output: before-and-after screenshots of one chart plus a one-line rationale for the change.
commonMistakes: Using a line chart for categories that have no time order, implying a trend that does not exist.
Leaving titles as labels ('Downtime by line') instead of messages ('Line 4 causes half of all downtime').
Keeping every series in full colour, so the audience cannot tell what to look at.

quickCheck.question: You want to show which five of 30 defect causes drive most rejects. Best chart?
options: Pie chart of all 30 causes
Pareto chart
Scatter plot
Stacked area chart
quickCheck.why: A Pareto ranks causes and shows cumulative contribution, making the vital few obvious.

quickCheck.question: What is the main problem with a dual y-axis chart?
options: It takes longer to build
The apparent crossing point and relative scale are arbitrary and can mislead
Excel does not support it
It cannot be printed in black and white
quickCheck.why: Two independent scales can be set to suggest a relationship that the data does not support.

quickCheck.question: What is the best use of a chart title in an OpEx review?
options: State the data source and date
Name the axes
State the message the audience should take away
Keep it blank to avoid leading the audience
quickCheck.why: A message title ensures the chart still communicates when read without you present.

OPEX-01.2.coachPrompt: Pick one chart you changed this month — what question does it answer now that it did not answer before?

OPEX-01.3.summary: This exercise walks you through building a defensible baseline and a credible target for one metric in your own function, then presenting both on a single slide. Without an agreed baseline, SCG improvement claims cannot be verified at year-end and savings are disputed by Finance.
objectives: You can define a baseline with a stated period, data source, scope and exclusions
You can set a target that is justified by a benchmark, entitlement or gap analysis rather than a round number
You can present baseline, target and gap on one chart that a sponsor can approve
keyPoints: A baseline needs four elements: metric definition, time window (usually 6–12 months to cover seasonality), data source, and documented exclusions.
State exclusions explicitly — planned shutdowns, trial runs, force majeure — and get them agreed before, not after, the improvement.
Justify the target from something external: best-demonstrated month, sister-plant performance, theoretical entitlement, or customer requirement.
Show the gap in business units (THB, tonnes, FTE-hours) and split it into what is in your control versus what is not.
Name the verification method and owner at the same time you set the target; agree with Finance who signs off the saving.
OPEX-01.3.scgExample: A chemicals shared-services team set a baseline for invoice processing: 'cost per invoice, Apr 2026–Mar 2027, from the SAP AP extract, excluding intercompany reposts' = THB 62 per invoice across 148,000 invoices. The best-demonstrated month was THB 51; the regional benchmark was THB 44. They set a 12-month target of THB 50, a gap of THB 1.78 million, and agreed with the Finance controller that verification would use the same SAP extract and exclusion rule each quarter.
OPEX-01.3.practiceTask: Choose one metric you own. Build a baseline slide containing: metric definition in one sentence, 12 months of data as a run chart, mean line, stated exclusions, target line with its justification, and the gap in THB. Then send it to one peer and one finance contact for challenge. Expected output: the slide plus a short note of the two strongest challenges received and how you answered them.
commonMistakes: Using a short or unusually bad period as the baseline, which inflates the apparent saving and destroys credibility.
Setting a round target (10% better) with no external justification.
Leaving exclusions undefined, so the baseline can be reinterpreted when results are reviewed.

quickCheck.question: Why is a 12-month baseline usually preferred to a 3-month one?
options: It produces a bigger number
It covers seasonality and normal variation
It is required by SCG policy
It reduces the need for a target
quickCheck.why: A full year captures seasonal and cyclical variation so the baseline is not an artefact of a good or bad quarter.

quickCheck.question: Which target justification is strongest?
options: A 10% improvement, as usual
The best-demonstrated month plus sister-plant performance
What the sponsor asked for in the meeting
The figure that makes the business case positive
quickCheck.why: Evidence from demonstrated performance shows the target is achievable with existing assets.

quickCheck.question: When should the verification method be agreed?
options: At the same time as the target
After the first quarter of results
Only if Finance asks
At project closure
quickCheck.why: Agreeing measurement up front prevents disputes about whether the saving is real.

OPEX-01.3.coachPrompt: Walk me through your baseline — what is excluded, who agreed the exclusions, and how would Finance verify the saving in month 12?

OPEX-02.1.summary: This 12-minute video shows a stripped-down value-stream mapping approach you can complete in one hour with the people who do the work. It matters at SCG because most waste sits in the handoffs between functions, which no single department's process map ever shows.
objectives: You can map a current-state flow of 8–12 steps with process time and wait time for each
You can calculate process cycle efficiency and identify the two largest delays
You can run the session with operators or clerks rather than mapping alone at your desk
keyPoints: Define start and end points and one product or transaction family before you draw anything; mixed families produce an unreadable map.
Capture two numbers per step: process time (hands-on work) and lead time (including waiting and queueing).
Process cycle efficiency = total process time / total lead time; in office processes it is often under 5%, which is where the opportunity lies.
Walk the flow physically or follow one real order end-to-end; do not rely on the documented procedure.
Mark information flows and decision loops — rework loops and approval waits are usually bigger than machine time.
OPEX-02.1.scgExample: A cement dealer-order team mapped 'order received to truck dispatched' for bulk orders in a 70-minute session with two clerks and a dispatcher. Total process time was 42 minutes; total lead time was 9.5 hours, a process cycle efficiency of 7%. The two largest delays were credit-hold release (4.1 hours, batch-checked twice a day) and manual weighbridge slip re-entry (1.8 hours of queueing). Both were invisible in the existing SOP.
OPEX-02.1.practiceTask: Book a 60-minute session with three people who run one of your processes end to end. Map 8–12 steps on a wall with sticky notes, writing process time and lead time on each. Calculate process cycle efficiency and circle the two largest waits. Expected output: a photo of the map, the efficiency figure, and a one-line hypothesis for each of the two biggest delays.
commonMistakes: Mapping from the written procedure instead of observing what actually happens.
Mixing several product or order types in one map, so no step has a meaningful time.
Recording only process time and missing the queues, which are usually 90% of lead time.

quickCheck.question: Process time is 30 minutes and lead time is 10 hours. What is process cycle efficiency?
options: Cannot be calculated
quickCheck.why: 30 minutes / 600 minutes = 5%... actually 30/600 = 5%, so the correct arithmetic gives 5%; 3% would require a 16-hour lead time.

quickCheck.question: Why map one product or transaction family at a time?
options: It is faster to draw
Mixed families give averaged step times that describe nothing real
Managers prefer simple maps
It avoids needing operators in the room
quickCheck.why: Different families follow different routes; averaging them hides the actual flow and timings.

quickCheck.question: Who should be in the mapping session?
options: The improvement team only
The people who actually perform the steps
Only managers who own the KPIs
External consultants
quickCheck.why: Only the people doing the work know the real waits, workarounds and rework loops.

OPEX-02.1.coachPrompt: What did your map show that the documented procedure did not, and who in the room was most surprised?

OPEX-02.2.summary: This reading explains how to convert observed waste into defensible THB figures that Finance will accept, using labour, material, energy, capacity and quality cost models. At SCG, improvement ideas compete for the same capital and attention, so an idea without a credible money figure rarely gets resourced.
objectives: You can select the right costing basis (cash, contribution margin or capacity) for a given waste
You can calculate the annualised value of one waste with stated assumptions
You can distinguish hard savings from cost avoidance and soft benefits when presenting
keyPoints: Match the basis to the situation: freed capacity on a sold-out line is worth contribution margin; freed labour hours are only cash savings if headcount or overtime actually falls.
Annualise carefully: value per event × events per month × 12, and state the event frequency source.
Quality waste = scrap material + conversion cost already added + rework labour + any customer penalty, not just material cost.
Energy and material waste use current unit prices with a stated reference date; note price volatility as a sensitivity.
Label every number: hard saving (hits the P&L), cost avoidance (spend not incurred), or capacity/soft benefit — and never sum the three into one headline.
OPEX-02.2.scgExample: A packaging line lost 118 hours a year to splice failures. The line runs at 9,000 sqm/hour with a contribution margin of THB 2.9/sqm, and it was sold out, so the loss was valued at capacity: 118 × 9,000 × 2.9 = THB 3.08 million of lost contribution. Separately, 6 tonnes of scrap paper at THB 14,500/tonne plus THB 210,000 of conversion cost already added gave THB 297,000 of hard material waste. The team presented THB 3.08m as capacity benefit and THB 297,000 as hard saving, not a combined THB 3.4m.
OPEX-02.2.practiceTask: Take the two largest delays or losses from your value-stream map or downtime Pareto. For each, write the costing basis, the formula, each input with its source, and the annualised THB value. Then ask your business partner in Finance to challenge the basis. Expected output: a half-page costing note per waste, with Finance's comment recorded.
commonMistakes: Valuing freed labour hours as cash savings when no headcount, overtime or contractor spend actually changes.
Using contribution margin for a line that is not capacity-constrained, which overstates benefit.
Adding hard savings, cost avoidance and soft benefits into a single headline figure.

quickCheck.question: A machine that is NOT capacity-constrained loses 100 hours. How should you value it?
options: Full contribution margin on lost output
Only the avoidable costs such as energy, materials and overtime incurred
Sales revenue of the lost output
Replacement cost of the machine
quickCheck.why: With spare capacity the output is not lost to the business; only avoidable spend is a real saving.

quickCheck.question: Which is a hard saving?
options: Two hours a week freed for a supervisor
Avoiding a future contractor hire
Overtime payments reduced by THB 40,000 per month
Faster order confirmation for dealers
quickCheck.why: Reduced overtime shows directly in the P&L as lower cash cost.

quickCheck.question: Scrap cost of a semi-finished product should include:
options: Material cost only
Material plus conversion cost already added plus rework labour
Selling price of the finished item
Material cost minus recycling value only
quickCheck.why: Value added before the defect is also lost; recovery value can then be deducted separately.

OPEX-02.2.coachPrompt: Show me one THB figure you calculated this month — what is the basis, and what did Finance say when you tested the assumption with them?

OPEX-02.3.summary: This exercise helps you design or repair a daily management routine: a short, standing, visual meeting where the team reviews yesterday's performance against target and assigns actions on abnormalities. Daily management is what keeps improvements from decaying once the project team leaves.
objectives: You can design a 15-minute daily meeting with a fixed agenda, board and owner
You can define abnormality triggers that decide when an issue is escalated rather than debated
You can run a two-week trial and adjust based on what the team actually uses
keyPoints: Fix the four elements: time and place, the board (3–6 metrics maximum), a standard agenda, and a named owner who runs it even when absent leaders are away.
Review only yesterday versus target; solve nothing longer than two minutes in the meeting — longer issues go to a named owner with a due date.
Define abnormality triggers in advance (e.g. any stop over 30 minutes, any customer complaint, any safety near-miss) so escalation is rule-based, not personality-based.
Keep an action log visible with owner and date; closing rate of actions is itself the health indicator of the routine.
Tier the routine: shift team at 07:30, department at 08:30, plant at 09:15, each escalating only unresolved items.
OPEX-02.3.scgExample: A cement packing plant ran a 15-minute 08:00 board review with four metrics: safety observations, bags packed versus plan, unplanned stop minutes, and moisture rejects. The trigger rule was any stop over 20 minutes or any reject batch. In the first two weeks 23 actions were raised and 17 closed within five days; unplanned stop minutes fell from an average 84 to 61 per day, mostly by fixing a recurring bag-feeder jam that had never been escalated before.
OPEX-02.3.practiceTask: Design a one-page daily management standard for your team: time, place, metrics (maximum six), agenda with timings, abnormality triggers, and action log format. Run it for five consecutive working days this week. Expected output: the one-page standard, a photo of the board after five days, and a count of actions raised versus closed.
commonMistakes: Putting 15 metrics on the board so nothing gets attention and the meeting overruns.
Turning the stand-up into a problem-solving session, which makes it long and people stop attending.
Reviewing weekly averages instead of yesterday, so abnormalities are spotted too late to investigate.

quickCheck.question: What should happen when an issue needs more than two minutes in a daily stand-up?
options: Extend the meeting until it is resolved
Assign a named owner and due date, and continue the agenda
Drop it as not important
Escalate it straight to the plant manager
quickCheck.why: The stand-up exists to detect and assign, not to solve; ownership with a date keeps it short and effective.

quickCheck.question: Why define abnormality triggers in advance?
options: To reduce the number of meetings
So escalation is rule-based rather than depending on who is in the room
To satisfy audit requirements
So the board can be automated
quickCheck.why: Pre-agreed triggers remove judgement and hesitation about when to raise an issue.

quickCheck.question: Which is the best health indicator of a daily management routine?
options: Attendance percentage
Number of metrics displayed
Rate and speed of action closure
How neat the board looks
quickCheck.why: Actions raised and closed on time show the routine is producing change, not just reporting.

OPEX-02.3.coachPrompt: After five days of your daily routine, which action would never have surfaced under your old weekly review, and what did it cost you before?

COMM-01.1.summary: A 12-minute video that maps the building materials value chain from quarry and clinker through grinding, bagging, logistics, dealers, contractors and end users, showing where cost sits and where margin is actually captured. It matters because SCG teams often optimise their own step while value leaks — or is created — two steps away.
objectives: You can name each step in the cement and building materials chain and state what it adds and what it costs
You can distinguish value created (willingness to pay) from value captured (margin retained) at each step
You can identify two points in your own chain where SCG captures less value than it creates
keyPoints: Value created = what the end customer will pay; value captured = what each partner keeps after its costs. They are rarely proportional.
Upstream (clinker, grinding) is capital- and energy-heavy: value comes from cost per tonne, kiln uptime and alternative fuel rate.
Midstream (logistics, bagging, warehousing) creates value through availability and lead time, not product difference — it is easily commoditised.
Downstream (dealer, applicator, specifier) captures value through access to the customer, credit, advice and installation service.
Margin pool = total profit in Baht available across the chain for a product; your share depends on scarcity of what you do and who owns the customer relationship.
Specification influence (architects, engineers, main contractors) shifts value before the order exists — it is the cheapest lever in the chain.
Services — mortar mix advice, on-site delivery scheduling, BIM support — create value that competitors cannot copy from a price list.
Chain steps with excess capacity lose pricing power; know which step in your chain is the bottleneck this year.
COMM-01.1.scgExample: A bagged mortar product sells to the homeowner at THB 165 per bag. SCG's ex-plant price is THB 112, the distributor sells at THB 132 and the sub-dealer at THB 148; the applicator adds THB 17 in labour markup embedded in the quoted job. SCG's cash cost is THB 94, so SCG captures THB 18 of the THB 71 chain margin while the two trade layers together capture THB 33. The team concluded that the biggest lever was not a price rise but reducing the two-layer structure to one in Nakhon Ratchasima, worth roughly THB 8 per bag on 400,000 bags a year.
COMM-01.1.practiceTask: Take one product or service line you touch. On one page, draw every step from SCG input to the paying end user. For each step write: the price it sells at, its rough cost, and one sentence on what it adds. Mark the step with the largest margin and the step you believe has most excess capacity. Output: a one-page chain map plus three bullets naming where SCG creates value it does not capture.
commonMistakes: Confusing revenue share with margin share — a step can move most of the money and keep almost none of the profit.
Stopping the map at the dealer instead of the end user who actually decides willingness to pay.
Treating logistics as pure cost when reliable delivery is often the value the dealer is paying for.
Assuming margin pools are fixed; they shift with capacity, fuel prices and substitute products.

quickCheck.question: A distributor buys at 112 and sells at 132, with 15 of handling and credit cost. What did it capture?
options: 20 per bag
5 per bag
132 per bag
Cannot be determined
quickCheck.why: Captured value is margin after its own cost: 132 − 112 − 15 = 5. The 20 is gross spread, not captured value.

quickCheck.question: Which step usually loses pricing power fastest in building materials?
options: Specification and technical advice
Steps with excess capacity and no product difference, such as basic transport
Kiln operation during a clinker shortage
Branded bagged products with installer loyalty
quickCheck.why: Commoditised steps with spare capacity have no scarcity, so customers can switch suppliers on price alone.

quickCheck.question: Why map to the end user rather than to the dealer?
options: Dealers dislike being the last step
Willingness to pay is set by the end user; everything upstream shares what they pay
Regulation requires end-user reporting
It makes the margin pool look larger
quickCheck.why: The total pool is defined by end-user price; without it you cannot see how the pool is split.

COMM-01.1.coachPrompt: Show me your chain map — which step captures the most margin per unit, and what would have to change for SCG to capture two Baht more without raising the end-user price?

COMM-01.2.summary: An 18-minute reading on how economics work between SCG and its partners — dealers, hauliers, converters, co-processing suppliers and JV partners — including margin sharing, credit, rebates, risk and switching costs. It matters because most commercial disputes at SCG are really unstated disagreements about who carries which cost and risk.
objectives: You can lay out a partner's P&L on your business in five lines: revenue, cost of goods, operating cost, working capital cost, net margin
You can explain how rebates, credit terms and consignment stock shift economics between SCG and the partner
You can propose one change to a partner deal that improves both sides' economics
keyPoints: A partner deal is three separate deals: the price deal, the cash deal (credit, payment terms) and the risk deal (stock, returns, warranty).
Calculate partner return on working capital, not just percentage margin. A 6% margin with 12 stock turns beats 12% with 3 turns.
Volume rebates paid late look cheap to SCG but are heavily discounted by a cash-tight dealer — an equivalent price cut may buy more loyalty for the same Baht.
Switching cost is what keeps a partner: shared systems, technical training, display stock, credit history. Low switching cost means annual price fights.
Shared-gain structures work only when the gain is measurable by both sides — e.g. delivery cost saved per drop, waste reduced per tonne.
Every concession you give should name the behaviour it buys: exclusivity, forecast accuracy, on-time payment, minimum drop size.
In packaging and chemicals, converter partners are exposed to resin or paper price swings; pass-through formulas remove a fight that neither side controls.
Test any deal for 'who is worse off if volume drops 20%' — that reveals where risk really sits.
COMM-01.2.scgExample: A packaging plant supplies corrugated boxes to a food converter at THB 14.20 per box on 60-day terms, with SCG holding two weeks of finished stock. The converter's stated ask was a 4% price cut. A quick five-line P&L showed its real pain was THB 2.1m tied up in stock and slow changeovers, not price. SCG instead moved to weekly call-off with 7-day lead time and kept price flat; the converter freed about THB 1.4m of working capital and signed a 2-year volume commitment, while SCG's finished-goods holding cost rose only THB 190,000 a year.
COMM-01.2.practiceTask: Pick one partner (dealer, haulier, converter or supplier). Reconstruct their P&L on your business in five lines using known prices plus reasonable estimates, and note their payment terms and stock days. Then write two options: one that costs SCG Baht, one that costs SCG little but improves the partner's cash or effort. Output: a half-page partner economics sheet with the two options and what behaviour each should buy.
commonMistakes: Negotiating only on unit price while ignoring terms, stock and returns, which often move more money.
Assuming the partner's margin equals the spread you can see, with no allowance for their freight, credit loss and handling.
Giving concessions without naming a measurable behaviour in return.
Designing shared-gain schemes on numbers only SCG can see, so the partner never trusts the payout.

quickCheck.question: A dealer earns 6% net margin and turns stock 12 times a year; another earns 12% and turns 3 times. Who earns more on the same capital?
options: The 12% dealer
The 6% dealer
They are equal
Depends on the brand
quickCheck.why: Return on capital ≈ margin × turns: 6×12 = 72 versus 12×3 = 36. Turns matter as much as margin.

quickCheck.question: What is the best test of where risk sits in a partner deal?
options: Who signed the contract first
Who is worse off if volume falls 20%
Who holds the trademark
Who pays the freight invoice
quickCheck.why: A demand-drop scenario exposes who carries stock, fixed cost and commitment risk.

quickCheck.question: Why may a delayed volume rebate be poor value per Baht spent?
options: It is taxed differently
A cash-constrained partner discounts future cash heavily, so it changes behaviour less than immediate price or terms
Rebates are illegal in Thailand
It cannot be audited
quickCheck.why: Partners short of working capital value cash now; the same Baht given as terms or price often buys more commitment.

COMM-01.2.coachPrompt: Walk me through your partner's five-line P&L — which line hurts them most, and does your current deal actually address that line?

COMM-01.3.summary: A 25-minute exercise where you build a dealer margin pool model for one product in one province and test three commercial interventions against it. It matters because dealer decisions at SCG are often argued on anecdote rather than on a simple numbers view that both sides could agree on.
objectives: You can build a per-unit margin pool for a product across SCG, distributor, sub-dealer and end user
You can quantify the effect of a rebate, a terms change and a route-to-market change on each party's margin
You can recommend one intervention with the Baht impact stated for SCG and the dealer
keyPoints: Build the pool per unit first, then multiply by realistic annual volume — never start with totals.
Include dealer costs that are invisible on the invoice: freight-in, breakage, stock days financed, bad debt, salesperson cost.
Model three levers separately: price/rebate, credit terms, and channel structure (layers removed or drop size changed).
Convert terms into Baht: extra credit days × unit cost × cost of capital ÷ 365.
Show the dealer's return on working capital, not just Baht per unit — it is the number the dealer's owner actually uses.
Sanity-check against reality: if your model says the sub-dealer earns 1% net, ask what else it earns (haulage, labour, cross-sell) before concluding it is irrational.
State the assumption you are least sure about and how much the answer moves if it is wrong by 20%.
End with one recommendation, one number and one behaviour asked of the dealer.
COMM-01.3.scgExample: For a 50kg bag in Khon Kaen: end-user 165, sub-dealer buys at 148, distributor buys at 132, SCG ex-plant 112 with cash cost 94. Distributor costs are freight-in 6, handling 3, 45 stock days financed at 7% (about 1.2) and 1% bad debt (1.3), leaving roughly 8.5 net. A modelled shift to direct supply of the 12 largest sub-dealers removed one layer on 180,000 bags: SCG raised realised price by 7 per bag but added 3.5 of freight and service cost, a net THB 630,000 gain, while participating sub-dealers gained about 4 per bag.
COMM-01.3.practiceTask: Using real prices from one product and one province, build the margin pool in a spreadsheet with a column per party and rows for price, visible costs, hidden costs and net margin. Then create three scenarios: 2% rebate, 30 extra credit days, and removing one channel layer for the top dealers. Output: a one-tab model plus five bullets stating the Baht impact per party per scenario and your recommendation with its key assumption.
commonMistakes: Ignoring hidden dealer costs so the dealer looks far more profitable than it is, which destroys credibility in the negotiation.
Comparing scenarios at different volumes, making the results non-comparable.
Expressing credit terms as days instead of Baht, so the cost is never weighed against a price concession.
Presenting only SCG's gain, leaving the dealer no visible reason to agree.

quickCheck.question: 30 extra credit days on a unit cost of 132 at 7% annual cost of capital is worth roughly how much per unit?
options: THB 0.76
THB 3.96
THB 9.24
THB 0.08
quickCheck.why: 132 × 7% × 30/365 ≈ 0.76 per unit — small per bag, but material across hundreds of thousands of bags.

quickCheck.question: Your model shows a sub-dealer at 1% net margin yet it keeps trading. What is the first thing to check?
options: The dealer is irrational
Other income streams and costs you omitted, such as haulage, labour supply or cross-sold products
Increase its rebate immediately
Terminate the dealer
quickCheck.why: An implausible result usually means a missing revenue or cost line, not irrational behaviour.

quickCheck.question: Which output makes a margin-pool recommendation usable in a dealer meeting?
options: A percentage margin comparison only
Baht impact for SCG and for the dealer, plus the behaviour requested
Total national volume figures
A list of competitor prices
quickCheck.why: Both parties need to see their own Baht outcome and what is expected in return for it to be agreed.

COMM-01.3.coachPrompt: Which assumption in your margin pool is weakest, and how would your recommendation change if it were 20% off?

COMM-02.1.summary: A 12-minute video introducing the vocabulary and economics behind SCG's Green, SVP (Service and Value Proposition) and HVA (High Value Added) offers, and how each earns a premium or defends volume. It matters because teams frequently label products 'green' or 'HVA' without being able to show where the extra Baht comes from.
objectives: You can define Green, SVP and HVA and give one SCG example of each
You can state the three ways a green or HVA offer earns money: price premium, volume access, cost avoided
You can identify which of the three applies to one offer in your own portfolio
keyPoints: HVA = product performance the customer will pay more for (strength, lighter weight, faster set, barrier properties). Proof is a specification or test result.
SVP = value delivered through service wrapped around the product (design support, scheduled delivery, take-back, on-site technical help). Proof is a saved cost or saved time for the customer.
Green = lower embodied carbon or circular content (lower clinker factor, recycled fibre, alternative fuel, recycled resin). Proof is a verified emission factor or recycled content figure.
Three money mechanisms: premium price, access to customers or tenders you would otherwise lose, and cost avoided (carbon levies, waste fees, penalties).
Green claims without third-party verification or a documented emission factor rarely earn a premium — they only avoid disqualification.
Cost-to-serve must be netted off: technical staff time, certification cost, smaller batch sizes and slower lines.
Green and HVA often combine: lower clinker factor can cut carbon and cost, but may need customer education on curing.
Volume defence is real value — quantify the tonnes at risk if the offer does not exist.
COMM-02.1.scgExample: A low-clinker cement variant carries an emission factor of 0.54 tCO2e per tonne versus 0.72 for the standard product. It costs THB 40 per tonne more to make, because of an additive and slower grinding. One precast customer pays a THB 90 per tonne premium to hit its own project carbon target, while a second refuses any premium but represents 24,000 tonnes a year that would go to a competitor without the low-carbon option. The offer therefore earns THB 50 per tonne on the first account and defends THB 24m of revenue on the second.
COMM-02.1.practiceTask: List the offers in your area that are labelled Green, SVP or HVA. For each, write the claim in one sentence, the proof available today, and which of the three money mechanisms it uses. Flag any offer with no proof and no mechanism. Output: a short table of offers with one line per offer and a shortlist of claims that need evidence before the next customer conversation.
commonMistakes: Calling something HVA because it is new or complex rather than because a customer pays more for its performance.
Ignoring the extra cost to serve, so a 'premium' offer is actually less profitable than the standard one.
Claiming carbon benefit without a documented emission factor or verification, which fails customer audits.
Overlooking volume defence, so the business case understates the value of a green option.

quickCheck.question: A green variant costs 40/tonne more and earns no premium, but keeps 24,000 tonnes of business at 300/tonne contribution. What is the value mechanism?
options: Price premium
Volume access / defence
Cost avoided
No value
quickCheck.why: The offer secures business that would otherwise be lost; that defended contribution is the value, net of the added cost.

quickCheck.question: Which best distinguishes SVP from HVA?
options: SVP is cheaper
SVP delivers value through service around the product; HVA through product performance
HVA applies only to chemicals
SVP requires certification
quickCheck.why: HVA is paid for in product specification; SVP is paid for in service outcomes such as time or cost saved for the customer.

quickCheck.question: What normally has to exist before a customer pays a green premium?
options: A marketing brochure
A verified emission factor or documented recycled content the customer can use in their own reporting
A competitor price list
An internal target
quickCheck.why: Customers pay when the claim is usable in their own carbon accounting or tender submission; unverified claims are not.

COMM-02.1.coachPrompt: Pick one offer you call green or HVA — what is the proof, and which of the three money mechanisms is it actually earning through?

COMM-02.2.summary: An 18-minute reading on the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and what it means practically for SCG exports of cement, clinker and related goods, including data requirements and where the cost lands. It matters because CBAM turns product carbon intensity into a direct price line on export invoices and requires plant-level data that must be assembled now.
objectives: You can explain how CBAM converts embedded emissions into a cost for an EU importer
You can list the data your plant or business unit must supply for a CBAM declaration
You can produce a rough exposure estimate in Baht for one export flow
keyPoints: CBAM applies to listed goods (including cement and clinker) imported into the EU; the EU importer buys certificates priced off the EU ETS, so the cost enters the landed price negotiation.
Exposure ≈ tonnes exported × embedded emissions per tonne × certificate price × (1 − free allocation phase-out factor), minus any verified carbon price already paid in Thailand.
Embedded emissions must be actual, installation-level data — direct process and fuel emissions plus specified indirect electricity emissions — not industry averages, once transitional reporting ends.
Data you need: production volume per installation, fuel and raw material consumption, clinker factor, electricity consumption and grid or PPA emission factor, and any purchased precursor emissions.
Poor data hurts twice: default values are conservative (high), and importers discount suppliers who cannot supply audit-ready figures.
Levers that reduce exposure: lower clinker factor, higher alternative fuel rate, renewable electricity with credible certificates, and product mix shifted toward lower-intensity grades.
Commercially, the question is who absorbs the cost. Treat it as a price negotiation item with a transparent calculation, not a hidden surcharge.
Build the data process into monthly routine reporting; annual scrambles produce numbers that cannot be verified.
COMM-02.2.scgExample: A business unit exports 40,000 tonnes of cement a year to two EU customers. At 0.68 tCO2e embedded per tonne and a certificate price of EUR 75, gross exposure is about EUR 2.04m, reduced to roughly EUR 0.61m in a year when 70% free allocation still applies. Cutting the clinker factor from 0.82 to 0.74 lowers embedded emissions to about 0.61 tCO2e per tonne and trims exposure by around EUR 55,000 at that phase-out level. The team agreed a quarterly data pack — fuel mix, clinker factor, grid factor — so the figures are defensible when importers ask.
COMM-02.2.practiceTask: Choose one export flow (product, destination, annual tonnes). Assemble the four inputs you can get this week: tonnes, embedded emissions per tonne (actual or best estimate), assumed certificate price, and current free-allocation factor. Calculate gross and net exposure, then list the data gaps and who owns each. Output: a half-page exposure note with one number, the assumptions behind it, and a named owner per data gap.
commonMistakes: Using industry average emission factors when installation-level actuals are required, producing a number that fails verification.
Forgetting indirect emissions from purchased electricity and precursor materials.
Ignoring the free-allocation phase-out schedule, which makes exposure look flat when it rises each year.
Treating CBAM as a compliance-only topic instead of a line in the customer price negotiation.

quickCheck.question: 20,000 t exported, 0.70 tCO2e/t embedded, certificate EUR 80, 50% free allocation remaining. Approximate net exposure?
quickCheck.why: 20,000 × 0.70 × 80 = EUR 1.12m gross; with 50% still freely allocated the adjusted exposure is about EUR 560,000.

quickCheck.question: Which data set is essential for a defensible CBAM figure?
options: Sales forecasts by region
Installation-level production, fuel, clinker factor and electricity consumption with emission factors
Dealer margin data
Competitor export volumes
quickCheck.why: CBAM requires actual installation-level emissions data, covering direct emissions and specified indirect electricity emissions.

quickCheck.question: Why does weak carbon data cost money even before certificates are surrendered?
options: Regulators fine the exporter directly
Default values are set conservatively high and importers discount unverifiable suppliers
Banks refuse letters of credit
Freight rates rise
quickCheck.why: Defaults are deliberately punitive and buyers prefer suppliers who can hand over audit-ready numbers.

COMM-02.2.coachPrompt: What is your current best estimate of CBAM exposure on your largest EU flow, and which single data gap most weakens that number?

COMM-02.3.summary: A 25-minute exercise in building and defending a price for a green or HVA option, covering cost to serve, willingness to pay, competitor alternative and the customer's own avoided cost. It matters because green offers at SCG are often either given away to win a trial or priced on internal cost with no link to customer value.
objectives: You can build a price range for a green option using cost floor, competitor reference and customer value ceiling
You can quantify the customer's avoided cost as the basis for a premium
You can write a two-line price rationale a sales colleague could use in a customer meeting
keyPoints: Set three anchors: floor (full cost to serve including certification and lost line speed), reference (best competing alternative for the customer), ceiling (customer's avoided cost or value gained).
Customer avoided cost is the strongest argument: carbon levy avoided, tender points won, waste disposal fee saved, rework or wastage reduced.
Price per unit of value where possible — Baht per tonne CO2e avoided makes the premium comparable to the customer's other abatement options.
If your premium exceeds the customer's cheapest alternative abatement route, expect rejection — know their alternatives.
Segment: some customers have hard carbon targets and will pay; others only need the option to exist. Do not offer one price to both.
Protect the standard product — a green premium that cannibalises HVA volume at lower margin is a loss.
Build in a review trigger: certificate prices, regulation and input costs move, so set a repricing date.
Write the rationale in two lines. If it cannot be said simply, it will be discounted in the room.
COMM-02.3.scgExample: A low-carbon cement costs THB 40/tonne more to produce plus THB 12/tonne of technical support, giving a floor of THB 52. A precast customer facing an EU-linked carbon cost estimates THB 640 avoided per tonne CO2e; the variant saves 0.14 tCO2e per tonne, implying a ceiling near THB 90/tonne. The nearest competitor blend is offered at a THB 70 premium with weaker verification. The team priced at THB 78/tonne with a verified emission factor attached, giving roughly THB 26/tonne contribution above the floor and a customer abatement cost of about THB 557 per tonne CO2e — cheaper than their next-best option.
COMM-02.3.practiceTask: Take one green or HVA offer and one named customer. Calculate your cost floor including all extra cost to serve, estimate the customer's avoided cost per unit, and find the competitor reference price. Convert your proposed premium into Baht per tonne CO2e avoided. Output: a one-page price sheet showing floor, reference, ceiling, recommended price, and a two-line rationale for the sales conversation.
commonMistakes: Cost-plus pricing that ignores what the option is worth to the customer, leaving money on the table or pricing above their alternative.
Omitting soft cost to serve — technical hours, certification, slower changeovers — so the floor is too low.
Using one price for all customers regardless of whether they have a binding carbon target.
Setting a premium without a review date, so it becomes stale when certificate prices or input costs move.

quickCheck.question: Your premium is THB 78/tonne and the option saves 0.14 tCO2e/tonne. What is the customer's abatement cost?
options: THB 78 per tCO2e
THB 557 per tCO2e
THB 10.9 per tCO2e
Cannot be calculated
quickCheck.why: 78 ÷ 0.14 ≈ 557 per tCO2e, the figure the customer compares against their other abatement options.

quickCheck.question: Which anchor sets the realistic ceiling for a green premium?
options: SCG's full cost to serve
The customer's avoided cost or next-best abatement option
Last year's list price
The plant's budget target
quickCheck.why: Customers will not pay more than the value gained or than their cheaper alternative route to the same outcome.

quickCheck.question: Why should the cost floor include technical support hours?
options: It is required by accounting policy
Green and HVA offers usually need advice and documentation; excluding it makes a loss-making price look profitable
It increases the premium automatically
Customers request it
quickCheck.why: Cost to serve is a real cash cost of the offer; omitting it understates the floor and can turn a premium into a loss.

COMM-02.3.coachPrompt: For your last green quote, what was the customer's cost per tonne of CO2e avoided, and how did that compare with their cheapest alternative?

SILO-01.1.summary: A 12-minute video on how to ask for, receive and act on feedback so that it changes behaviour rather than just being logged. It matters at SCG because most supervisors get honest input only from their own function, and the blind spots that slow cross-unit work sit exactly where that input is missing.
objectives: You can ask a specific, answerable feedback question instead of 'any comments for me?'
You can respond to critical feedback without defending, using a three-step listen-check-commit reply
You can convert one piece of feedback into a visible behaviour change and close the loop with the giver
keyPoints: Feedback lands when it is requested, specific and timed close to the event - within 48 hours of the meeting or handover.
Replace open invitations with a narrow ask: 'In yesterday's S&OP meeting, what did I do that made it harder for logistics to raise the delay?'
Use listen-check-commit: listen without interrupting, check by paraphrasing back, commit to one concrete change.
Defensiveness is usually the first sentence you say. Practise a neutral opener: 'That's useful - tell me more about where you saw it.'
Cross-function feedback is riskier for the giver; lower their cost by asking in private, thanking them, and never re-litigating the point later.
Act on one thing, not five. A single visible change builds more credibility than a long improvement list.
Close the loop: tell the giver what you changed. This is what turns a one-off comment into a continuing source.
Level 3 behaviour is seeking feedback from people who do not report to you and whose targets conflict with yours.
SILO-01.1.scgExample: A production supervisor at the Saraburi cement plant noticed that the logistics team stopped raising truck-turnaround issues in the weekly meeting. Instead of a general request, he asked the logistics planner one question: 'When I pushed back on the 14:00 dispatch change last week, what did that signal to your team?' The planner said his tone made it sound like the plant schedule was non-negotiable. He committed to one change - opening each weekly meeting by asking logistics for constraints first - and told the planner two weeks later that truck waiting complaints raised in-meeting had gone from zero to four.
SILO-01.1.practiceTask: Pick one cross-functional colleague you worked with in the last two weeks. Ask them one narrow feedback question about a specific interaction, using listen-check-commit. Write half a page: the question you asked, what you heard verbatim, the one behaviour you will change, and the date you will report back to them. Bring this to the clinic.
commonMistakes: Asking 'do you have any feedback for me?' at the end of a meeting - too broad and too public to get an honest answer.
Explaining the context before the person finishes, which the giver reads as defending and stops the conversation.
Collecting feedback from five people and changing nothing, which trains people not to bother next time.
Only asking people inside your own function or your own reporting line, where the answers are already comfortable.

quickCheck.question: Which feedback request is most likely to produce a usable answer?
options: 'Let me know if you have any feedback on my leadership.'
'In Tuesday's handover, what did I do that made it hard for you to flag the quality issue?'
'Was the meeting OK for you?'
'Please complete my 360 form by Friday.'
quickCheck.why: It names a specific event and a specific behaviour, so the giver can answer without having to generalise or judge the person.

quickCheck.question: A peer from finance says your reports are always late and it disrupts their close. What is the best first response?
options: Explain that the plant data arrives late from SAP.
Say 'That's useful - tell me more about where that hits you.'
Agree to send everything two days earlier from now on.
Ask who else has complained.
quickCheck.why: Listen and check first. Explaining or over-committing immediately both cut off the information you still need.

quickCheck.question: What most reliably turns feedback into a reputation change?
options: Recording it in your development plan
Sharing it with your line manager
Making one visible change and telling the giver what you changed
Asking more people the same question
quickCheck.why: Closing the loop on a single concrete change is what the other person actually observes, and it keeps the feedback channel open.

SILO-01.1.coachPrompt: Who gave you feedback this month that you did not enjoy hearing, what exactly did you change because of it, and how did they find out?

SILO-01.2.summary: A short reading on how different SCG functions are shaped by their own metrics, time horizons and risk tolerance, and how to read those styles instead of reading intent. It matters because most 'difficult people' across silos are simply people optimising a different, legitimate scorecard.
objectives: You can describe the metric, time horizon and main risk of two functions you depend on
You can reframe a recurring conflict as a style or incentive difference rather than a personality problem
You can adapt how you frame a request so it fits the other function's decision logic
keyPoints: Style follows incentive. Plant operations is judged on uptime and safety, sales on volume and customer promise, finance on accuracy and control, procurement on cost and supply continuity.
Time horizon differs sharply: operations thinks in shifts, sales in weeks, finance in monthly close and quarters, capital projects in years.
Risk tolerance differs: an ops leader will not gamble on safety; a sales leader will not gamble on a lost customer. Neither is wrong.
Detail norms differ. Engineering expects data before a decision; commercial expects a decision then refinement. Mismatched norms feel like obstruction.
Frame your ask in the other side's currency: tell logistics the impact on truck turnaround, tell finance the impact on accrual accuracy.
Ask 'what does good look like on your scorecard this quarter?' early in any cross-function relationship - before you need something.
Style-reading is not agreement. You still negotiate, but you negotiate about trade-offs rather than about attitudes.
At Level 3 you can explain function B's position to function A more fairly than they can explain it themselves.
SILO-01.2.scgExample: A packaging plant manager kept clashing with the credit team over holding shipments to a corrugated-box customer with a 45-day overdue balance of THB 3.2 million. He assumed credit was being bureaucratic. After one conversation about their scorecard - bad-debt provision and days sales outstanding - he changed his framing from 'this customer is important' to 'here is a payment plan that cuts DSO by nine days and keeps the volume.' Credit released the shipment within a day and the pattern of escalation to the business head stopped.
SILO-01.2.practiceTask: Choose the function you argue with most. Write a one-page profile: their top two KPIs this year, their planning horizon, the two risks their head loses sleep over, and their evidence norms. Fill what you can from memory, then book a 20-minute call with a counterpart to correct it. Output: a corrected profile plus one sentence on how you will reframe your next request.
commonMistakes: Treating a functional constraint as a personal attitude, which pushes the discussion into escalation instead of trade-offs.
Building the profile from assumption only and never validating it with the other function.
Using style labels as excuses ('finance is just like that') rather than adapting your framing.
Framing every request in your own metrics and expecting the other side to translate.

quickCheck.question: Sales repeatedly commits delivery dates the plant cannot meet. The most useful first interpretation is:
options: Sales does not respect operations
Sales is measured on order intake and customer promise, with a weekly horizon
Sales needs training on production planning
The planning system is wrong
quickCheck.why: Starting from their scorecard and horizon explains the behaviour and opens a trade-off discussion rather than a blame discussion.

quickCheck.question: You need a capex approval quickly from finance. Best framing?
options: Emphasise how urgent it is for your team
Lead with payback period, cash phasing and the control risk of not acting
Escalate to the business head
Send the full engineering specification
quickCheck.why: Framing in finance's own currency - cash, return and control risk - fits their decision logic and reduces rework.

quickCheck.question: What is the best evidence that you have reached Level 3 on reading working styles?
options: You can name the four style types
You avoid conflict with other functions
You can state another function's position fairly enough that they agree with your summary
You attend cross-function meetings regularly
quickCheck.why: Being able to represent another function's case accurately shows genuine understanding rather than vocabulary or avoidance.

SILO-01.2.coachPrompt: Describe the last cross-function disagreement you had from the other side's scorecard - what would they say they were protecting, and did you check that with them?

SILO-01.3.summary: A 25-minute exercise to design a personal operating rhythm: the fixed pattern of time, contacts and feedback loops that keeps you connected outside your own function. It matters because cross-silo relationships decay silently unless they are scheduled, and most managers only meet other functions when there is already a problem.
objectives: You can map where your working week currently goes by function and by activity type
You can design a weekly and monthly rhythm that includes at least two recurring cross-function touchpoints
You can build one standing feedback loop into your calendar and protect it for a quarter
keyPoints: Audit before design: two weeks of calendar data usually shows 80-90% of meeting time inside your own function.
A rhythm has three layers - daily (team check), weekly (cross-function touchpoint), monthly (feedback and review).
Cross-function time should be booked when there is no crisis; problem-only contact makes every conversation adversarial.
