Name the loop: one recurring 20-minute slot with a specific counterpart beats a vague intention to 'connect more'.
Protect the rhythm by making it visible - published in your calendar, known to your team, and not the first thing cancelled.
Build in one slot per month for reviewing feedback received and checking whether your committed change is holding.
Rhythm is a Level 2 to Level 3 bridge: it turns feedback-seeking from an event into a habit others can rely on.
Review the rhythm quarterly; drop touchpoints that produce nothing rather than letting them decay into ritual.
SILO-01.3.scgExample: A shared-services payroll supervisor audited four weeks of her calendar and found 34 of 38 meeting hours were inside HR shared services. She added two recurring slots: 20 minutes every Tuesday with the Rayong chemicals HR business partner, and 30 minutes monthly with the plant admin lead. Within one quarter, off-cycle payroll corrections from that site fell from 19 to 6 per month because issues were raised before cut-off rather than after. She dropped a third touchpoint with procurement after six weeks when it produced no actions.
SILO-01.3.practiceTask: Export your last four weeks of calendar entries. Tag each by function (own / other) and type (decide, inform, build relationship). Calculate the percentage of time spent outside your function. Then design a one-page rhythm: daily, weekly and monthly slots, with named counterparts and one standing feedback loop. Book the first four weeks of slots before the clinic. Output: the audit numbers and the booked calendar.
commonMistakes: Designing an ambitious rhythm with six new meetings that collapses in three weeks - start with two.
Booking cross-function time as 'open' slots with no named person or purpose, so nothing is prepared.
Cancelling the cross-function slot first whenever operations gets busy, which signals it was never real.
Never reviewing the rhythm, so dead touchpoints continue to consume time while new needs go unserved.

quickCheck.question: Your calendar audit shows 92% of meeting time inside your own function. The best first move is:
options: Cancel half your internal meetings
Add two named recurring cross-function slots and protect them
Ask your manager for a role change
Join three cross-functional project teams
quickCheck.why: Small, named and protected additions are sustainable; mass cancellation or large project commitments usually fail within weeks.

quickCheck.question: Why should cross-function touchpoints be scheduled outside crisis periods?
options: Crises are handled by senior managers anyway
Contact only during problems makes every interaction adversarial and removes early warning
Calendars are emptier during quiet periods
It looks better in the development plan
quickCheck.why: Routine contact is what surfaces issues before they escalate and keeps the relationship usable when pressure rises.

quickCheck.question: What belongs in the monthly layer of a personal operating rhythm?
options: Daily shift handover
Reviewing feedback received and checking whether your committed change is holding
Approving overtime
Weekly production meeting
quickCheck.why: The monthly layer is for reflection and follow-through on feedback, which the daily and weekly layers cannot absorb.

SILO-01.3.coachPrompt: Show me your calendar for the last three weeks - which cross-function slots did you keep, which did you cancel, and what did the kept ones actually produce?

SILO-02.1.summary: A 12-minute video on aligning priorities when two functions hold different, equally valid targets. It matters at SCG because most cross-silo delay is not disagreement on facts but unresolved trade-offs that no one names out loud.
objectives: You can surface the specific trade-off behind a cross-function stand-off in one sentence
You can run a short alignment conversation that ends in a named decision, owner and date
You can escalate a genuine trade-off with options rather than with a complaint
keyPoints: Most 'misalignment' is two people optimising different KPIs correctly - name the KPIs first, before the solution.
State the trade-off explicitly: 'We can hold the 48-hour delivery promise or protect the kiln maintenance window, not both this week.'
Alignment needs a shared object: one number, one date, one customer commitment that both sides agree to be measured on.
End every alignment conversation with decision, owner, date. Without these three, you have had a discussion, not an alignment.
Escalate with two options and a recommendation, not with a problem. Senior time is for choosing, not for discovering.
Distinguish alignment (we agree the trade-off and the choice) from compliance (they do it because you pushed harder).
Write the agreement in two lines and send it within the hour. Memory diverges fast across functions.
At Level 3 you align functions you have no authority over by making the trade-off and its cost visible.
SILO-02.1.scgExample: A cement distribution manager and a plant scheduler deadlocked over a THB 4.1 million dealer order due Friday against a planned two-day mill shutdown. Instead of escalating, the distribution manager named the trade-off: 'Either we release 3,000 tonnes from the Ang Thong buffer at THB 180,000 extra freight, or we push the dealer to Monday and risk the account.' They chose the buffer, recorded the decision, owner and date in two lines, and sent it to both heads. The escalation that would have taken three days was closed in 40 minutes.
SILO-02.1.practiceTask: Identify one cross-function issue currently stuck on your list. Write the trade-off in one sentence naming both KPIs at stake. Prepare two options with cost and risk for each, plus your recommendation. Hold a 30-minute conversation with your counterpart this week and record decision, owner and date. Output: the one-sentence trade-off and the three-line decision record.
commonMistakes: Debating solutions before naming which two targets are actually in conflict, so the conversation loops.
Ending with 'we'll coordinate' or 'let's keep in touch' instead of a decision, owner and date.
Escalating a raw complaint upward, which sends the problem back down for options anyway.
Treating a win by authority as alignment - the other function complies once and resists next time.

quickCheck.question: Which sentence best surfaces a cross-function trade-off?
options: 'Logistics is not cooperating on the dispatch plan.'
'We can meet the dealer's 48-hour promise or protect the maintenance window this week, not both.'
'We need better coordination between plant and logistics.'
'Can we discuss the dispatch schedule tomorrow?'
quickCheck.why: It names both competing commitments and the time frame, which is what allows a choice to be made.

quickCheck.question: An alignment meeting ends with everyone agreeing the issue is important. What is missing?
options: A follow-up meeting
Decision, owner and date
Senior management attendance
A written business case
quickCheck.why: Without a named decision, a single owner and a date, agreement in the room does not change what happens next week.

quickCheck.question: You must escalate a genuine trade-off to your business head. Best form?
options: A summary of the disagreement and who is blocking
Two options with cost and risk, plus your recommendation
A request for the head to decide the priority for the year
A meeting invitation with both functions present
quickCheck.why: Escalating with options and a recommendation lets the decision be made in one step instead of being sent back for analysis.

SILO-02.1.coachPrompt: Take a cross-function issue you closed this month - what was the trade-off in one sentence, and who owned the decision by what date?

SILO-02.2.summary: A reading on making decision rights explicit - who recommends, who decides, who must be consulted and who is simply informed. It matters because a large share of rework at SCG comes from decisions that were made twice, or not at all, because rights were assumed rather than agreed.
objectives: You can map decision rights for a recurring decision in your area using a simple recommend-decide-consult-inform model
You can spot the two failure patterns: no clear decider, and too many consult rights
You can renegotiate one decision right with a counterpart and document it
keyPoints: Four roles are enough: recommend (does the analysis), decide (single named person), consult (must be heard before), inform (told after).
One decider. If two names sit in the decide box, you have an escalation machine, not a decision.
Consult is expensive - each consult right adds days. Limit it to those who carry real risk from the decision.
Inform is not weaker; it is the right default for people who need visibility but not a veto.
Map the decision type, not the department: 'price exception above 5%' is a decision; 'commercial matters' is not.
Unclear rights show up as symptoms: decisions reopened, meetings without conclusions, approvals sought after the fact.
Agree rights when things are calm and write them down; renegotiating mid-crisis costs credibility on both sides.
Level 4 behaviour is redesigning a set of recurring decisions so the standard applies beyond your own team.
SILO-02.2.scgExample: In a chemicals business, customer price exceptions above 5% were discussed by sales, credit and the product manager, with no named decider; average turnaround was 6.5 working days. The team mapped it: sales recommends, product manager decides, credit consults if the account is overdue, plant is informed. Consult rights dropped from four functions to one conditional trigger. Turnaround fell to 1.5 days over the next quarter and reopened decisions stopped.
SILO-02.2.practiceTask: Pick one recurring decision in your area that regularly stalls. Map it on one page: decision statement, who recommends, the single decider, who is consulted and why, who is informed, and the target turnaround time. Test the map against the last three times that decision was made. Output: the map plus a note of every place reality differed from the map.
commonMistakes: Mapping departments instead of specific decisions, which produces a chart nobody can apply.
Putting two or three names in the decide box to avoid upsetting people, which reinstates the original problem.
Granting consult rights broadly as a courtesy, adding days of delay for no risk reduction.
Agreeing the map verbally and never writing it down, so the old pattern returns within a month.

quickCheck.question: A decision map lists both the plant manager and the logistics manager as deciders. The likely result is:
options: Faster decisions through shared ownership
Routine escalation to the next level when they disagree
Better quality decisions
Clearer accountability
quickCheck.why: Two deciders means no decider; disagreements have no resolution point and default to escalation.

quickCheck.question: Which function should hold a consult right on a credit-limit exception?
options: Every function that touches the customer
Only those carrying real risk from the decision, such as credit
All managers at the same grade
Anyone who asks to be included
quickCheck.why: Consult rights add days each; they should be limited to parties who bear actual risk from the outcome.

quickCheck.question: Which symptom most clearly indicates unclear decision rights?
options: Long meeting agendas
The same decision being reopened weeks later by a different function
High workload in the team
Frequent emails from other functions
quickCheck.why: Reopened decisions signal that the original decider was never genuinely agreed or communicated.

SILO-02.2.coachPrompt: Which recurring decision did you map this month, and what happened the first time someone tried to reopen it outside the map?

SILO-02.3.summary: A 25-minute exercise in designing and running a 15-minute cross-functional stand-up that keeps a shared commitment on track. It matters because standing cross-silo forums, done badly, become status theatre; done well, they remove blockers within a day instead of a week.
objectives: You can design a 15-minute stand-up with a fixed agenda, fixed attendees and a single shared number
You can run the meeting so that every blocker leaves with an owner and a date
You can kill or redesign a stand-up that stops producing decisions
keyPoints: One shared number at the top of every stand-up - on-time delivery, open claims, days to close - visible to all functions.
Fixed slot, fixed people, 15 minutes standing or on camera. Attendance by named deputy if the person cannot attend.
Three questions only: what moved since yesterday, what is blocked, what needs a decision today.
Blockers are logged live with owner and date; anything needing more than three minutes goes to a separate short call.
No presentations, no slide packs. The shared number and the blocker log are the whole material.
Rotate the facilitator across functions after the first month - it shifts ownership away from a single silo.
Measure the meeting itself: count blockers raised and average days to clear. If clearance time stops improving, redesign it.
Level 3 is running one well; Level 4 is setting the format as the standard across several teams and showing the impact number.
SILO-02.3.scgExample: A packaging plant ran a daily 15-minute stand-up with production, quality, logistics and customer service on one number: same-day dispatch rate, then at 78%. Blockers were logged live - pallet shortage, a pending QC release, a truck booking gap - each with an owner and a same-day deadline. Average blocker clearance fell from 3.2 days to 0.8 days over eight weeks and the dispatch rate reached 91%. When the quality representative started sending a different person each day, the facilitator reset the named-deputy rule.
SILO-02.3.practiceTask: Design a stand-up for one shared commitment in your area. Write a one-page charter: the shared number and its current value, the four to six named attendees and deputies, the fixed slot, the three questions and the blocker-log format. Run it at least three times this week. Output: the charter plus the blocker log showing owner, date and clearance time for each item.
commonMistakes: Letting the stand-up become a status update round, where each function reports and nothing is decided.
Inviting too many people, so the meeting stretches past 15 minutes and senior attendees stop coming.
Logging blockers without an owner and a date, which turns the log into a complaints list.
Keeping the stand-up running out of habit after the shared number has stopped moving.

quickCheck.question: What is the single most important design element of a cross-functional stand-up?
options: A detailed slide pack prepared by the host function
One shared number visible to all functions at the top of every session
Attendance by senior managers
A 45-minute slot to cover all topics
quickCheck.why: A single shared number gives the functions a common object to align on and prevents the meeting sliding into parallel status reports.

quickCheck.question: A blocker is raised that needs 20 minutes of technical discussion. What should the facilitator do?
options: Work through it in the stand-up
Name an owner and a date, and move it to a separate short call
Defer it to next week's stand-up
Escalate it immediately
quickCheck.why: The stand-up surfaces and assigns blockers; solving them in the room destroys the time box and the attendance.

quickCheck.question: Blocker clearance time has been flat at three days for six weeks. The right response is:
options: Add more attendees
Extend the meeting length
Review whether the right deciders are present and redesign or stop the stand-up
Report the problem upward
quickCheck.why: A flat clearance time usually means the people with decision rights are not in the room; the meeting should be redesigned or ended rather than continued as ritual.

SILO-02.3.coachPrompt: Show me your blocker log from the last two weeks - how many items had a named owner and date, and what happened to your average clearance time?

CUST-01.1.summary: A 12-minute video on how to run a structured 30-minute interview with an internal customer of a shared services team (HR, Finance, IT, Procurement) to surface real needs rather than stated solutions. It matters because most shared services improvements at SCG are scoped from ticket volumes and assumptions, not from what the receiving function actually needs.
objectives: You can prepare a 6-question interview guide that opens with the internal customer's job, not your service
You can distinguish a stated solution from the underlying need and probe behind it
You can write up an interview in a one-page note with verbatim quotes and a needs list
keyPoints: Interview the person who does the work, not only their manager — the pain lives at the transaction level
Open with 'walk me through the last time you...' so you get behaviour, not opinion
When they ask for a solution ('add a field to the form'), ask 'what would that let you do?' twice
Silence is a tool: after their answer, wait three seconds before the next question
Capture verbatim quotes; paraphrase loses the emotional signal that ranks priorities
Close with 'what have I not asked about that matters?' and 'who else should I talk to?'
Validate within 48 hours: send back your summary and ask them to correct it
Five to seven interviews per internal customer group is usually enough to see repeats
CUST-01.1.scgExample: The Shared Services payroll team assumed plant HR officers wanted a faster ticket response, because 62% of tickets were chased at least once. Six interviews with HR officers at Saraburi and Rayong showed the real need: they could not tell a requester when the correction would appear on the payslip, so they chased to have something to say. The fix was a visible expected-completion date on the ticket, not more headcount. Chase-up contacts fell from 62% to 24% of tickets in two months with no change in actual resolution time.
CUST-01.1.practiceTask: Pick one internal customer group your team serves. Book and run two 30-minute interviews this week using a 6-question guide that starts with their work, not your service. Write one page per interview: three verbatim quotes, a list of needs stated as 'I need to ... so that ...', and one assumption of yours that was wrong. Bring both pages to the clinic.
commonMistakes: Demoing or defending your service during the interview, which turns discovery into a sales call
Interviewing only the manager who signs the SLA rather than the daily user
Writing up only conclusions and discarding quotes, so the evidence cannot be re-examined
Treating the first solution request as the requirement and building it

quickCheck.question: An internal customer says 'just give us a monthly extract in Excel'. What is the best next move?
options: Add it to the backlog as a requirement
Ask what they would do with the extract, and what they do today instead
Explain why the BI dashboard is better
Ask them to raise a formal service request
quickCheck.why: The extract is a proposed solution. Asking what it enables reveals the underlying need, which may be met more cheaply or differently.

quickCheck.question: Why send your interview summary back to the interviewee within 48 hours?
options: To create an audit trail for the SLA
To validate that you understood the need and to keep the relationship open
Because policy requires written records of all meetings
To get their manager's sign-off
quickCheck.why: Validation is the second half of needs discovery; unchecked notes drift into the interviewer's own assumptions.

quickCheck.question: You have done seven interviews and the last two raised nothing new. What does that suggest?
options: The interview guide is too narrow
You have probably reached saturation for this group and can move to synthesis
You need at least fifteen interviews to be valid
The sample was biased toward senior staff
quickCheck.why: Repetition without new themes is the practical signal to stop interviewing that group and start synthesising.

CUST-01.1.coachPrompt: Tell me about one thing an internal customer said in your interviews that contradicted what your team believed — and what you changed because of it.

CUST-01.2.summary: A reading on planning and running discovery interviews with external B2B customers — contractors, converters, brand owners, distributors — where commercial relationships and buying committees complicate honest answers. It matters because SCG's B2B customers rarely volunteer unmet needs to the person who also negotiates their price.
objectives: You can map a customer's buying committee and choose who to interview for which question
You can run a discovery interview that stays separate from a commercial negotiation
You can triangulate what a customer says against what their order and complaint data shows
keyPoints: Separate the discovery conversation from price talk, explicitly and at the start, or you will only hear discount requests
Map at least three roles per account: the user (site foreman, line operator), the buyer (procurement), the influencer (technical or QA)
Anchor on their economics: waste rate, downtime, rework, cash tied up — B2B needs are usually cost or risk in disguise
Bring your own data as a prompt, not as proof: 'we see 4 returns from your site last quarter — walk me through one'
Ask about the process either side of your product: what happens to the pallet before and after it touches them
Interview lost and lapsed accounts as well as top accounts; the strongest needs signal sits with people who left
Two interviewers is better: one asks, one records verbatim and watches for non-verbal reaction
Triangulate: a stated need that no behaviour supports is a preference, not a need
CUST-01.2.scgExample: A packaging sales team believed its corrugated box customers wanted shorter lead times, since 'lead time' appeared in most QBR decks. Interviews with three line supervisors and two procurement leads at a food converter in Bang Pakong showed lead time was fine; the pain was pallet-to-pallet moisture variation that caused 1.8% crush loss on the filling line in the rainy season. Order data confirmed it — claims clustered in June to September. The team piloted a moisture-controlled wrap for two accounts, cutting reported crush loss to 0.6% and winning a 12-month commitment worth THB 38 million.
CUST-01.2.practiceTask: Choose one external account you know well. Draw its buying committee (names, roles, what each cares about). Book one 30-minute discovery call this week with a user-level contact you have not interviewed before, with price explicitly off the agenda. Produce a one-page note: three needs stated as 'I need ... so that ...', and for each, one data point from your own systems that supports or contradicts it.
commonMistakes: Interviewing only the procurement contact, who is trained to talk about price and terms
Letting the account manager both interview and defend past service issues in the same meeting
Accepting a stated need with no supporting behaviour or data as a confirmed requirement
Skipping lapsed customers because the conversation is uncomfortable

quickCheck.question: A contractor says your delivery is 'always late', but your data shows 94% on-time to the confirmed slot. What is the right response?
options: Correct them with the on-time figure
Ask them to walk you through the last late delivery and what it cost them
Escalate to logistics for a root-cause review
Record 'delivery reliability' as the top need
quickCheck.why: The gap between perception and data is the finding. Walking through a specific incident usually reveals a different definition of 'on time' — often notification, not arrival.

quickCheck.question: Why interview lapsed accounts during B2B discovery?
options: To win them back during the interview
They give the clearest unmet-need signal because they acted on it
Their data is easier to access
Regulators expect churn analysis
quickCheck.why: Customers who left have already voted with their order book; their reasons are the least diluted by relationship politeness.

quickCheck.question: What most reliably keeps a discovery interview from turning into a negotiation?
options: Holding it at the customer's site
Saying at the start that pricing is out of scope and bringing no commercial documents
Using a written questionnaire
Having the country manager attend
quickCheck.why: Explicit scoping plus removing commercial artefacts changes the customer's frame from bargaining to explaining.

CUST-01.2.coachPrompt: Which need from your B2B interviews did your own transaction data fail to support, and how did you resolve the contradiction?

CUST-01.3.summary: A 25-minute exercise converting raw interview findings into testable requirements with an owner, a measure and an acceptance condition. It matters because most SCG improvement projects stall between the insight deck and the work order, where 'customers want faster service' cannot be built or verified.
objectives: You can rewrite a raw customer statement into a need, then into a requirement with a measurable acceptance condition
You can rank requirements by customer impact against effort and state what you will not do
You can trace every requirement back to at least two pieces of interview evidence
keyPoints: Three-layer chain: verbatim quote → need ('I need X so that Y') → requirement ('the service must do Z, verified by measure M')
A requirement without a measure and a threshold is a wish; add the number even if it is a first guess
Keep traceability: each requirement lists the quote IDs behind it, so you can defend or drop it later
Separate must-have (customer cannot work without it) from should-have (removes friction) from nice-to-have
Requirements state outcomes, not designs — 'requester can see expected completion date' not 'add a field to SAP screen 3'
Write explicit non-requirements: what you heard and consciously chose not to address, and why
Frequency plus severity beats loudness; one angry director is not a requirement
Re-validate the top five requirements with two original interviewees before committing resources
CUST-01.3.scgExample: After eight interviews on cement bulk delivery scheduling, a team had 41 raw statements. They collapsed these into 9 needs and 6 requirements; the top one read: 'A site can confirm or reschedule a bulk slot up to 4 hours before arrival, with confirmation received in under 2 minutes, verified by 90% of reschedules completed without a phone call.' Two requirements about invoice formatting were logged as non-requirements with the reason 'mentioned twice, low severity, owned by Finance'. The single measurable requirement replaced a previous 24-slide 'improve customer experience' brief and was scoped by IT in one workshop.
CUST-01.3.practiceTask: Take the interview notes from CUST-01.1 or 01.2. Build a three-column table for at least 12 raw statements: quote → need → requirement with measure and threshold. Then rank the requirements must/should/nice, and write three explicit non-requirements with reasons. Expected output: a one-page requirements table you can hand to a process or IT owner without further explanation.
commonMistakes: Writing the solution you already wanted into the requirement column
Dropping traceability so nobody can tell which requirements came from customers and which from the team
Leaving thresholds blank because 'we don't have the data yet' — estimate and mark it provisional
Ranking by how senior the person who complained was, rather than frequency and severity

quickCheck.question: Which is a properly written requirement?
options: Improve responsiveness to dealer enquiries
Build a chatbot for dealer enquiries
Dealers receive a substantive reply to a stock enquiry within 2 working hours, 95% of the time
Dealers are frustrated by slow replies
quickCheck.why: It states an outcome, a measure and a threshold, and is neutral about the design that delivers it.

quickCheck.question: What is the purpose of writing explicit non-requirements?
options: To meet documentation standards
To show stakeholders their input was heard and record why it is out of scope
To reduce the number of interviews needed
To transfer the work to another department
quickCheck.why: Recorded exclusions prevent scope creep later and preserve trust with the people who raised them.

quickCheck.question: Two interviewees mention an issue; one director mentions a different issue forcefully. How should you rank them?
options: Director's issue first — sponsorship matters
Assess both on frequency and severity, and be explicit about any sponsor override
Drop the director's issue as a sample of one
Split resources equally
quickCheck.why: Evidence-based ranking is the discipline; if seniority overrides it, that should be a visible decision rather than a hidden one.

CUST-01.3.coachPrompt: Show me one requirement from your table and walk me back to the two quotes behind it — then tell me what you decided not to do.

CUST-02.1.summary: A 12-minute video on how AI lead and opportunity scoring works for CBM's dealer channel, what data it needs, and how a sales supervisor should use a score without outsourcing judgement to it. It matters because CBM sales teams cover hundreds of dealers with limited visit capacity, and visit allocation is still mostly habit-driven.
objectives: You can explain what a dealer propensity score is, what features drive it, and what it cannot tell you
You can use a ranked dealer list to plan a week of visits and say why you overrode the ranking
You can name the data quality and fairness checks to run before trusting a score
keyPoints: A score is a ranked probability, not a verdict: it says 'this dealer is more likely to respond', not 'this dealer will buy'
Typical features: order recency and frequency, basket mix shift, credit utilisation, territory construction starts, response to last promotion, service complaints
Garbage in: duplicate dealer records and stale contact ownership degrade scores faster than any modelling choice
Always compare against a baseline — last quarter's revenue ranking — or you cannot tell if the model adds anything
Watch for feedback loops: if reps only visit high-scored dealers, the model never learns about the rest; hold back a random 10% control group
Scores decay; a dealer score older than 4 weeks in a seasonal market is close to useless
Keep the reason codes visible to reps ('score up: basket shifted to mortar, credit headroom 40%'), or adoption collapses
Human override is a feature, not a failure — log the override reason and feed it back
CUST-02.1.scgExample: A CBM regional team scored 420 dealers in the Northeast for likelihood of increasing dry-mortar volume in the next 60 days. Reps worked the top 120 plus a randomly chosen 40-dealer control group. Over the quarter, conversion in the scored group was 27% versus 11% in the control, while average visit count per rep stayed at 38. Two of the top-scored dealers were overridden by the supervisor because of unresolved credit disputes — the override reason was logged and credit status was added as a feature in the next refresh.
CUST-02.1.practiceTask: Export your dealer list with the last 12 months of order data. Build a simple manual score in a spreadsheet: rank dealers on three features you can justify (e.g. order frequency change, basket breadth, credit headroom), weight them, and produce a top-20 list. Compare it with the top 20 by revenue. Expected output: the two lists side by side, plus a short note on which dealers appear only in the score list and why they are worth a visit.
commonMistakes: Treating the score as a target ('visit everyone above 0.7') instead of a prioritisation aid
Scoring on revenue history alone, which just re-ranks your existing big accounts
Skipping the control group, so improvement cannot be attributed to the model
Hiding reason codes from reps, who then quietly revert to their own dealer lists

quickCheck.question: Why keep a randomly selected control group of dealers outside the scored call plan?
options: To reduce rep workload
To measure whether the score actually improves conversion and to keep the model learning
Compliance requires a holdout
To give junior reps easier accounts
quickCheck.why: Without a holdout you cannot separate model effect from seasonality or rep effort, and the model stops seeing data on unvisited dealers.

quickCheck.question: A dealer scores high but has a frozen credit line. What should the supervisor do?
options: Visit anyway, the model is data-driven
Override, log the reason, and raise credit status as a missing feature
Remove the dealer from the CRM
Lower all scores in that province
quickCheck.why: Logged overrides are how business constraints get encoded into the next model version instead of eroding trust in it.

quickCheck.question: Which is the weakest basis for a dealer propensity score?
options: Change in basket mix over two quarters
Total revenue in the last 12 months only
Credit headroom
Response to the previous promotion
quickCheck.why: Historic revenue alone mostly reproduces the existing account ranking and adds little new prioritisation information.

CUST-02.1.coachPrompt: Which dealer did the score rank highly that you would never have visited — and what happened when you did?

CUST-02.2.summary: A reading on building B2B account segmentations that a sales and marketing team will actually use, including where AI clustering helps and where simple rules are better. It matters because SCG BUs often run three conflicting segmentations at once — by revenue, by industry code and by sales region — and none of them changes what anyone does on Monday.
objectives: You can choose between rule-based and AI-derived segmentation for a given decision
You can build a segmentation whose segments differ in behaviour, not just in size
You can define the action and the owner attached to each segment before you publish it
keyPoints: Start from the decision: 'how do we allocate service cost' and 'which accounts get a technical rep' need different segmentations
Rule-based (size × growth × margin) is transparent, auditable and enough for most coverage decisions
AI clustering earns its place when you have many behavioural variables and no obvious cut points — order patterns, product mix, service intensity, payment behaviour
Test segment validity: segments must differ meaningfully on outcomes you care about, and members should stay in their segment for at least two quarters
Four to six segments is the practical ceiling; beyond that, sales teams cannot remember them
Name segments by behaviour ('project-driven bulk buyers'), not by letter or tier, so the name implies the action
Every segment needs an owner, a coverage model and a cost-to-serve target, or it is just a chart
Re-run and review quarterly; publish the migration table showing which accounts moved and why
CUST-02.2.scgExample: A chemicals BU clustered 310 converter accounts on eight behavioural variables and found five segments. One — 'spec-sensitive small runs', 62 accounts, 9% of volume — had 3.1 technical support calls per order against a portfolio average of 0.6, and negative margin after service cost. Rather than dropping them, the BU moved the segment to a self-serve technical library plus quarterly clinics, cutting support calls to 1.2 per order and turning the segment margin-positive within two quarters. The segmentation was reviewed quarterly; 14 accounts migrated out in the first review.
CUST-02.2.practiceTask: Take your account list and build a rule-based segmentation using three axes you can defend (e.g. annual volume, 12-month growth, service intensity). Produce 4–6 named segments with account counts, revenue share and average cost-to-serve. For each segment write one sentence: what we do differently and who owns it. Expected output: a one-page segment table with named actions, plus a list of the 5 accounts hardest to classify and why.
commonMistakes: Building segments that differ in size but behave identically, so no action changes
Letting AI produce 11 clusters and shipping all of them to the sales team
Segmenting once and never re-running, so the model ages past usefulness
Publishing segments without an owner or a coverage decision attached

quickCheck.question: What is the first test of a useful B2B segmentation?
options: Segments are roughly equal in revenue
Different segments warrant genuinely different actions
It uses a machine learning algorithm
It matches the sales region structure
quickCheck.why: Segmentation exists to differentiate treatment; if every segment gets the same coverage, the exercise added nothing.

quickCheck.question: When is AI clustering preferable to a rule-based segmentation?
options: Whenever more data is available
When there are many behavioural variables with no obvious natural cut points
When the audit team requires transparency
When the account base is under 50
quickCheck.why: Clustering earns its complexity in high-dimensional behavioural data; simple, auditable rules are better where cut points are known.

quickCheck.question: An account moves segment every quarter. What does that most likely indicate?
options: The customer is growing fast
The segmentation variables are too volatile or the account sits on a boundary
The sales rep is mis-coding data
The segment count is too low
quickCheck.why: Stable membership over two or more quarters is a validity check; constant migration signals volatile variables or borderline placement.

CUST-02.2.coachPrompt: For your largest segment, what do your team now do differently that they did not do before the segmentation?

CUST-02.3.summary: A 25-minute exercise designing and pricing a differentiated offer for one customer segment using AI assistance for variant generation, then stress-testing it for margin and cannibalisation. It matters because AI makes it cheap to generate dozens of offer variants and expensive to discover, three months later, that the winning variant simply discounted existing volume.
objectives: You can construct an offer with a clear value exchange rather than a straight discount
You can use an AI assistant to generate and critique offer variants while keeping margin control
You can calculate breakeven uplift and cannibalisation risk before launch
keyPoints: Every offer is an exchange: what the customer gets, what they commit (volume, term, data, payment behaviour), and what it costs you
Use AI to generate 8–10 variants fast, then screen manually on margin, operational feasibility and channel conflict
Ask the AI to argue against your favourite variant — cannibalisation, gaming, competitor response
Compute breakeven uplift: at a 6% discount on a 22% gross margin, you need roughly 38% volume uplift just to hold gross profit
Prefer non-price levers where possible: delivery slot priority, technical support hours, extended terms tied to on-time payment, bundled logistics
Define eligibility precisely so existing committed volume cannot simply re-badge itself as incremental
Pilot on a limited account set with a control group, fixed end date and pre-agreed kill criteria
Never paste customer-identifiable or contract-price data into general-purpose AI tools; use anonymised structures and approved internal tools
CUST-02.3.scgExample: For the 'project-driven bulk buyers' segment, a CBM team used an internal AI assistant to generate nine offer variants from an anonymised brief. Screening left three; the finance check showed the headline 5% volume rebate needed 31% incremental volume to break even on a 19% gross margin, which historic elasticity did not support. They launched instead a guaranteed 24-hour delivery slot plus site technical visit in exchange for a 3-month rolling forecast, piloted on 25 dealers against a 25-dealer control. Incremental volume was 14% with margin intact, and forecast accuracy improved enough to cut emergency haulage by THB 1.2 million in the quarter.
CUST-02.3.practiceTask: Pick one segment from CUST-02.2. Write a 150-word anonymised brief (segment behaviour, cost-to-serve, margin band, constraints) and ask an approved AI assistant for 8 offer variants plus a critique of the two you like best. Then build a one-page offer sheet: value exchange, eligibility rule, breakeven uplift calculation, cannibalisation risk, pilot design with control group and kill criteria. Expected output: the offer sheet plus the AI prompt you used.
commonMistakes: Going straight to a discount because it is the easiest variant to model
Pasting real customer names, volumes or contract prices into a public AI tool
Skipping the breakeven calculation and judging the pilot on revenue rather than gross profit
Writing eligibility loosely, so baseline volume qualifies as incremental

quickCheck.question: Gross margin is 22% and you offer a 6% price discount. Roughly what volume uplift is needed to hold gross profit?
options: About 6%
About 15%
About 38%
About 100%
quickCheck.why: New margin is 16%; you need 22/16 ≈ 1.375, i.e. roughly 38% more volume just to stand still.

quickCheck.question: What is the safest way to use a general AI assistant in offer design?
options: Upload the account master file for context
Work from an anonymised segment brief with margin bands, not customer-identifiable data
Use it only after legal sign-off on the offer
Avoid AI entirely for commercial work
quickCheck.why: Anonymised briefs give the assistant enough structure to be useful without exposing customer or contract data.

quickCheck.question: Which design element most protects against cannibalisation?
options: A shorter pilot period
Precise eligibility rules defining what counts as incremental volume
A larger discount to drive clear uplift
Limiting the offer to one region
quickCheck.why: Cannibalisation happens when existing volume qualifies; tight eligibility definitions are the primary control.

CUST-02.3.coachPrompt: What was the breakeven uplift on your chosen offer, and what evidence do you have that the segment can actually deliver it?

CHG-01.1.summary: This 12-minute video shows how to convert a vague improvement idea into four hard elements: a measured baseline, a dated target, one named owner and a fixed review cadence. Without these four, SCG improvement sprints drift and the claimed benefit cannot be verified at closure.
objectives: You can state a baseline with its measurement window, data source and unit
You can write a target in the form 'from X to Y by date' for your own improvement
You can name a single accountable owner and explain what they decide versus what they escalate
keyPoints: Baseline = the actual current level, measured over a period long enough to cover normal variation (usually 8-13 weeks), not last month's best number.
Always record three things with the baseline: data source, who pulls it, and the unit. If you cannot name the source, you do not have a baseline.
A target is 'from X to Y by date'. 'Improve significantly' or 'reduce complaints' is not a target.
One owner, not a committee. Co-owners mean nobody prepares the number before the review.
Cadence follows the signal speed: daily data → weekly review; monthly closing data → monthly review. Reviewing faster than the data refreshes creates noise.
Separate the outcome metric (what the business feels) from one or two process metrics (what the team controls week to week).
Write down what you will NOT measure, to stop the scorecard growing to 15 rows.
Agree the closure rule up front: how many consecutive periods at target count as 'done'.
CHG-01.1.scgExample: A packaging plant in Rayong wants to cut corrugated sheet waste. The team pulls 13 weeks of ERP scrap data and sets the baseline at 4.6% waste on the flexo line, source = daily production log consolidated by the process engineer. The target becomes 'from 4.6% to 3.4% by 31 March', owner = the flexo shift supervisor, cadence = Tuesday 09:00 for 20 minutes with the plant manager. Process metric: number of setup jobs using the new register-check sheet, target 100% of setups.
CHG-01.1.practiceTask: Take one improvement you are currently running. In 25 minutes, fill a one-page card with: baseline number, measurement window, data source and data puller; target in 'from X to Y by date' form; one named owner; one outcome metric plus one process metric; review day, time and length; and the closure rule. Bring the card to the clinic. Expected output: a single page where every field has a number or a name, no blanks, no 'TBD'.
commonMistakes: Using a single recent month as baseline, which usually flatters or exaggerates the problem and makes the later gain unprovable.
Setting the target before checking whether the data source can actually produce the number every review cycle.
Naming a department ('Logistics') as owner instead of a person, so no one prepares the evidence.
Choosing weekly cadence for a metric that only updates at month-end close, which turns reviews into speculation.

quickCheck.question: Which statement is a usable target?
options: Reduce truck turnaround time as much as possible this year
Reduce average truck turnaround from 78 to 60 minutes by 30 June
Improve truck turnaround through better coordination
Benchmark truck turnaround against other plants
quickCheck.why: It gives a start point, an end point and a date, so progress and closure can be judged objectively.

quickCheck.question: Your cost data only closes monthly. What cadence fits?
options: Daily stand-up on the cost metric
Weekly review of the cost metric
Monthly review of cost, with weekly review of a process metric you control
Quarterly review only
quickCheck.why: Match review frequency to data refresh for the outcome, and use a faster process metric to steer in between.

quickCheck.question: What must be recorded alongside the baseline number?
options: The target only
Measurement window, data source and who pulls it
The list of team members
The budget approved
quickCheck.why: Without window, source and owner of the pull, the baseline cannot be reproduced or defended at closure.

CHG-01.1.coachPrompt: Show me your baseline number and tell me who pulled it, from which system, and over what period — then tell me what changes if that number turns out to be wrong.

CHG-01.2.summary: This reading explains how to run a short weekly review where the evidence, not the commentary, drives decisions. It matters because most SCG improvements fail quietly in the gap between the kick-off meeting and the closure report.
objectives: You can run a 20-minute weekly evidence review with a fixed agenda and pre-published data
You can distinguish a status update from an evidence review and convert one into the other
You can decide each week between continue, adjust, escalate or stop, and record the reason
keyPoints: Evidence cadence means the number arrives before the meeting. If the first time anyone sees the data is on the screen in the room, it is a status meeting, not an evidence review.
Fixed slot, fixed length, fixed agenda: metric vs target, what moved and why, blockers, next week's commitments. 20 minutes is enough for one improvement.
Every week ends with one of four decisions — continue, adjust the countermeasure, escalate, or stop — written in one line with a date.
Track leading process metrics weekly; the outcome metric may lag by weeks and that is normal. State the expected lag up front so a flat outcome does not trigger panic.
Commitments are written as 'who does what by when', maximum three per week. More than three means the team is not choosing.
Keep a single running log rather than new slide decks. The log is the audit trail at closure.
Missing data is itself a finding: if the number could not be pulled, that becomes the top blocker for the week.
Attendance discipline matters more than attendance size: owner plus the people who can remove blockers. Others read the log.
CHG-01.2.scgExample: A cement dealer support team is reducing order-entry errors. Every Monday 16:00 the coordinator publishes a two-line update by 15:00: errors last week 41 versus baseline 63 and target 25, and 86% of orders used the new confirmation template. In week 4 the error count rose to 48; the log showed template use had dropped to 52% because two new staff were untrained, so the decision was 'adjust — train both by Thursday, owner Nok'. By week 7 errors were 29 and the team kept the cadence for four more weeks before closing.
CHG-01.2.practiceTask: This week, run one 20-minute evidence review on your own improvement. Before the meeting, publish the metric versus target and one process metric to attendees at least an hour ahead. In the meeting, capture: what moved, why, top blocker, the weekly decision, and up to three 'who/what/when' commitments. Expected output: one filled log row plus a note on what you had to change to get the data published in advance.
commonMistakes: Presenting narrative progress ('team is engaged, workshops held') instead of the metric against target.
Letting the review drift to 45 minutes by solving problems in the room instead of assigning them.
Cancelling the review when the data looks bad — exactly the week the review is most needed.
Carrying open actions forward silently week after week without changing owner, date or approach.

quickCheck.question: What is the clearest sign your weekly review is a status meeting rather than an evidence review?
options: It lasts 20 minutes
The data is shown for the first time during the meeting
The owner chairs it
It uses a standing agenda
quickCheck.why: Evidence reviews require the number to be circulated beforehand so the meeting spends its time on decisions.

quickCheck.question: The outcome metric is flat after three weeks but the process metric is at 95% adoption. Best response?
options: Stop the improvement as ineffective
Continue, if the expected lag between adoption and outcome has not yet passed
Change the target to match the flat result
Add five more metrics to find movement
quickCheck.why: Outcomes lag adoption; the agreed lag assumption tells you whether flatness is expected or a real signal.

quickCheck.question: How many commitments should a weekly review produce?
options: As many as the team can list
At most three, each with owner and date
One per attendee
None; commitments belong in the monthly review
quickCheck.why: A short list with named owners and dates is what actually gets done between reviews.

CHG-01.2.coachPrompt: Walk me through your log for the last four weeks — which week did you decide to adjust, and what number told you to?

CHG-01.3.summary: A structured 25-minute exercise in which you draft and stress-test a one-page impact contract for a live improvement. It matters because the contract is what your sponsor signs, what the review uses each week, and what proves the benefit at closure.
objectives: You can draft a complete one-page impact contract covering baseline, target, owner, cadence, benefit and closure rule
You can stress-test a peer's contract with five challenge questions and fix the weakest field
You can state how the claimed benefit will be verified and by whom
keyPoints: The contract has seven fields: problem in one sentence, baseline, target, owner, cadence, benefit (money or risk or time), and closure rule.
Benefit must be traceable to a line someone recognises: cost per tonne, overtime hours, days sales outstanding, complaint count. Vague 'efficiency' benefits get discounted at closure.
Name the verifier — usually finance, cost control or a process owner outside the team — and agree the verification method before you start.
Add an assumptions box: what must stay true (volume, headcount, no line rebuild) for the target to be reachable.
Stress-test questions: Where does the number come from? What if it moves for reasons other than us? Who says it's done? What do we stop doing? What breaks if the owner is on leave?
One page only. If it needs two pages, the scope is too large — split it.
Sign-off means the sponsor accepts the cadence and the data source, not just the target.
CHG-01.3.scgExample: A chemicals site drafts a contract to cut analytical lab rework: baseline 11.2% of samples rerun over 12 weeks, target 6% by 30 September, owner = lab section head, cadence Thursday 08:30, benefit = 340 technician hours per quarter released, verified by the site cost controller from the LIMS rerun report. Stress-testing revealed the LIMS report did not separate customer-requested reruns, so the team added a filter and restated the baseline to 9.4%. The assumptions box recorded 'sample volume stays within ±10% of 2026 average'. Closure rule: three consecutive months at or below 6%.
CHG-01.3.practiceTask: In 25 minutes, draft the seven-field contract for one live improvement, then swap with a peer and apply the five stress-test questions to each other's page. Fix the single weakest field on your own page and note what changed. Expected output: a signed-off-ready one-pager plus two lines describing the field you corrected and why the stress test caught it.
commonMistakes: Claiming a financial benefit that finance has never agreed to recognise, so the result is disputed at closure.
Leaving out the assumptions box, then blaming a volume swing when the target is missed.
Writing a closure rule like 'when the target is hit once', which lets a lucky month end the improvement too early.
Scoping one contract across three departments so no single owner can be accountable.

quickCheck.question: Who should verify the claimed benefit?
options: The improvement owner, since they know the detail best
A party outside the team such as cost control or the process owner
The sponsor, at closure only
Nobody; the metric speaks for itself
quickCheck.why: Independent verification of the data and the money makes the claim credible outside the team.

quickCheck.question: What is the purpose of the assumptions box?
options: To list the team members
To record conditions that must hold for the target to be achievable
To describe the countermeasures
To capture the budget
quickCheck.why: It makes context dependencies explicit so later variance can be explained honestly rather than argued.

quickCheck.question: A contract runs to three pages. Best action?
options: Reduce the font size
Split the scope into separate improvements with their own owners
Remove the baseline section
Keep it; detail shows rigour
quickCheck.why: Length usually signals scope too broad for one owner and one cadence; splitting restores accountability.

CHG-01.3.coachPrompt: Which field of your impact contract would your sponsor challenge first, and what evidence do you have ready for it?

CHG-02.1.summary: This 12-minute video covers what to do in the two weeks after an improvement sprint ends: turning the new way of working into documented standard work with a named process owner. It matters because most SCG regressions happen when the sprint team disbands and the old method quietly returns.
objectives: You can convert a proven countermeasure into a one-page standard with trigger, steps, and what to do when it fails
You can identify which existing routine (shift handover, monthly review, audit) will carry the standard
You can name the process owner who maintains the standard after the project owner leaves
keyPoints: A sprint proves a method works; standard work makes it the default for people who were never in the sprint.
Minimum viable standard: trigger (when to use it), the steps, the record it leaves behind, and the escalation when the step cannot be done.
Attach the standard to an existing routine rather than creating a new meeting — shift handover, pre-start check, month-end checklist, internal audit scope.
Update the artefacts people actually use: the checklist, the SAP transaction note, the form, the training matrix. Not the project slide deck.
Train by observing the first three real uses, not by circulating the document.
Transfer ownership explicitly and on a date: project owner to line process owner, with the sponsor witnessing.
Build in a decay check: who looks at adherence in 30, 60 and 90 days, and what triggers a re-intervention.
If the standard makes the job harder, it will be bypassed. Remove an old step whenever you add a new one.
CHG-02.1.scgExample: After a four-week sprint, a cement plant's packing line cut bag-breakage from 1.8% to 0.9% using a revised sealer temperature check. The team wrote a one-page standard: trigger = every shift start and after any product change; three steps; record on the existing shift handover sheet; escalate to the maintenance planner if temperature drift exceeds 4°C. They deleted the old manual log to keep the workload neutral, and ownership passed to the packing section head on 1 July with 30/60/90-day adherence checks by the plant quality engineer.
CHG-02.1.practiceTask: Take one improvement your team completed in the last six months. In 25 minutes, write its one-page standard (trigger, steps, record, escalation), name the existing routine that carries it, name the process owner, and list one old step you will delete. Then check whether the current artefacts (checklist, form, system note) actually reflect the new method. Expected output: the one-pager plus a list of artefacts that still describe the old way.
commonMistakes: Declaring the sprint finished at the closing presentation without assigning a process owner or a carrying routine.
Adding the new step while leaving all old steps in place, so the team drops the new one under time pressure.
Writing a five-page SOP nobody reads instead of a one-page standard at the point of work.
Training by email attachment rather than observing the first real executions.

quickCheck.question: Which is the strongest way to make a new practice stick?
options: Announce it in a town hall
Attach it to an existing routine and update the checklist people already use
Create a new weekly meeting to monitor it
Add it to the annual policy manual
quickCheck.why: Embedding in routines and artefacts already in daily use requires no extra discipline to survive.

quickCheck.question: When should ownership move from the project owner to the line process owner?
options: Only if the project owner leaves the company
On a named date shortly after the sprint, witnessed by the sponsor
At the next annual planning cycle
Never; the project owner stays accountable
quickCheck.why: An explicit, dated handover prevents the accountability gap where regression usually starts.

quickCheck.question: What should a minimum viable standard contain?
options: Background, stakeholder map and benefit case
Trigger, steps, the record it leaves, and escalation when it fails
A full process flow diagram with swimlanes
Only the steps, to keep it short
quickCheck.why: These four elements are what an operator needs at the point of work to perform and flag problems.

CHG-02.1.coachPrompt: For the improvement you finished last quarter, who owns the standard now, and which routine touches it every week?

CHG-02.2.summary: This reading explains how to design a small set of sustain metrics — adherence, outcome and one early-warning signal — and where to publish them so regression is visible within weeks. It matters because at SCG scale, an improvement that decays unnoticed for six months costs more than one that was never attempted.
objectives: You can select an adherence metric and an outcome metric for a completed improvement and set a trigger level for each
You can place sustain metrics into an existing management routine instead of a standalone report
You can define the re-intervention rule that fires when a metric breaches its trigger
keyPoints: Three metrics are enough: adherence (are we doing it?), outcome (is it still working?), and one early-warning signal that moves first.
Adherence is the sustain metric most teams skip, yet it is the one that predicts regression — outcome deterioration shows up later.
Every sustain metric needs a trigger level and a named responder, e.g. 'adherence below 90% for two consecutive weeks → section head reviews within five working days'.
Move sustain metrics into a routine that already exists and already has consequences: plant daily meeting, monthly function review, internal audit checklist.
Set an explicit retirement date. After 6-12 months of stability, retire the adherence metric and keep only the outcome, or the scorecard becomes unmanageable.
Beware metric decay dressed as data problems: when a metric stops being reported, treat it as a red status, not a blank.
Define the metric so gaming is visible — count completed checks with timestamps, not self-declared percentages.
Publish the same number to the team who does the work, not only upward to management.
CHG-02.2.scgExample: A shared-services accounts payable team automated invoice matching, cutting manual touches from 62% to 24% of invoices. Sustain metrics: adherence = share of invoices routed through the new workflow (trigger: below 85% for two weeks), outcome = manual touch rate (trigger: above 30% in any month), early warning = number of workflow exceptions per day. All three sit on the existing AP daily board and the monthly function review; the responder is the AP team lead, escalating to the service manager. Adherence fell to 79% in October because a new vendor category bypassed the workflow, and the fix was made in four days before the outcome metric moved at all.
CHG-02.2.practiceTask: Pick one completed improvement in your area. In 25 minutes define its adherence metric, outcome metric and one early-warning signal, each with a data source, trigger level, named responder and response time. Then identify the existing meeting or report where all three will appear, and set a retirement date for the adherence metric. Expected output: a three-row sustain table with no blank cells, plus the name of the routine that will carry it.
commonMistakes: Tracking only the outcome, so decay is detected a quarter after adherence collapsed.
Defining triggers without a named responder or response time, so a red metric is discussed but nothing happens.
Creating a separate sustain report that nobody opens after month two.
Letting the sustain scorecard grow with every completed project because no metric ever retires.

quickCheck.question: Why is an adherence metric important alongside the outcome metric?
options: It is easier to collect
It moves before the outcome and gives time to intervene
Management prefers percentages
It replaces the need for audits
quickCheck.why: Adherence is a leading indicator; outcome deterioration confirms the problem only after it has cost something.

quickCheck.question: A sustain metric has not been reported for two months. How should it be treated?
options: As green, since no problems were raised
As blank, pending data
As red, because loss of visibility is itself a regression risk
As retired
quickCheck.why: Unreported metrics usually mean the routine has lapsed, which is exactly when practices slide back.

quickCheck.question: What makes a trigger level actionable?
options: It is set at a round number
It has a named responder and a response time attached
It is approved by the sponsor
It is reviewed annually
quickCheck.why: A threshold without an owner and a deadline produces discussion rather than correction.

CHG-02.2.coachPrompt: Show me the sustain metrics for one of your closed improvements — when did one last go red, and what happened within five days?

CHG-02.3.summary: A 25-minute exercise in which you build and rehearse the handover pack that transfers a completed improvement to its permanent owner. It matters because an unrehearsed handover leaves the receiving manager holding a target they did not set and cannot evidence.
objectives: You can assemble a handover pack containing standard, metrics, known failure modes and open risks
You can run a 15-minute handover conversation that ends in explicit acceptance or a named gap
You can agree a 30/60/90-day support arrangement with the receiving owner
keyPoints: Handover pack, five items: the one-page standard, the sustain metric table, the data-pull instructions, known failure modes with countermeasures, and open risks or unfinished items.
Handover is a conversation with an acceptance decision, not an email with attachments. The receiver either accepts, or names the gap and the date it will be closed.
Include the data-pull instructions in operational detail: system, report name, filters, frequency, who has access. Access rights are the most common silent failure.
List failure modes honestly — including the ones you did not solve. Hiding them destroys the receiver's trust in the numbers.
Agree tapering support: project owner attends the first month's reviews, is on call in month two, fully out by month three.
Update the training matrix and the job description or task list of the receiving role, so the work survives the individual.
Close the loop with the sponsor: a one-line record that the improvement was handed over on a date, with the accepting owner named.
CHG-02.3.scgExample: A dealer-channel team finishing a credit-check improvement hands over to the regional credit supervisor. The pack includes the revised two-step check standard, three sustain metrics, and exact pull instructions ('SAP report ZCR12, filter region = North, run every Monday; access requested via role CRD_RPT'). Known failure modes list month-end volume peaks when staff skip step two, with the agreed countermeasure of a temporary second reviewer. In the 15-minute handover the supervisor accepted three of four items but flagged she had no ZCR12 access, so the gap was logged and closed in two days; the project owner joined the next four Monday reviews then stepped out.
CHG-02.3.practiceTask: Choose an improvement you need to hand over in the next quarter. In 25 minutes assemble the five-item pack (one page each is enough) and write the 15-minute handover agenda, ending with an explicit acceptance question. Test the data-pull instructions by asking the receiving owner to pull the number themselves. Expected output: the pack, plus a note of any access or capability gap the test revealed and the date it will be closed.
commonMistakes: Handing over by email and assuming silence equals acceptance.
Omitting known failure modes so the new owner is ambushed by the first month-end peak.
Documenting the data pull without checking the receiver has system access or a licence.
Withdrawing entirely on handover day instead of tapering support over 30/60/90 days.

quickCheck.question: What must a handover conversation end with?
options: Thanks and a closing slide
An explicit acceptance, or a named gap with a closure date
A sponsor sign-off on the benefit
A new project charter
quickCheck.why: Without a stated acceptance or a logged gap, accountability is ambiguous from day one.

quickCheck.question: Which item is most often missing from handover packs?
options: The benefit case
Workable data-pull instructions including system access
The project timeline
The stakeholder map
quickCheck.why: Receivers frequently cannot reproduce the metric because access or report detail was never transferred.

quickCheck.question: How should known but unsolved problems be handled at handover?
options: Left out to avoid undermining confidence in the result
Listed as failure modes with countermeasures or as open risks
Mentioned verbally only
Reopened as a new sprint before handover
quickCheck.why: Explicit failure modes let the new owner prepare, and honesty protects the credibility of the reported result.

CHG-02.3.coachPrompt: Ask the person who received your improvement to pull this week's metric in front of you — did it work first time?

BB-01.1.summary: This 12-minute video shows how to run a structured framing conversation with a business sponsor so a vague idea becomes a written problem statement with a customer, a measurable gap and clear decision boundaries. At SCG most new concepts stall not because the idea is weak but because sponsor and team never agreed what problem is being solved or what would count as success.
objectives: You can write a one-page problem statement covering customer, current pain, size of gap and success measure
You can run a 30-minute sponsor framing conversation using a fixed question set
You can name the constraints (budget, timeline, no-go areas) a sponsor must confirm before work starts
keyPoints: Frame the problem as a customer pain with a number attached, not as a solution ("dealers wait 3 days for stock confirmation", not "build an app")
A usable frame has five parts: who has the problem, what it costs them, why now, what success looks like in numbers, and what is out of scope
Ask the sponsor for the decision they will make, not just the outcome they want — the frame must feed a gate decision
Confirm constraints early: budget ceiling, time to first evidence, channels or customers that are off limits, and internal politics
Separate assumption from fact in the frame; mark each claim as evidence-backed or to-be-tested
Play the frame back in writing within 24 hours and get a yes/no, not a nod in the meeting
Re-frame is normal — agree with the sponsor how often you will return with revised framing (typically every 2-3 weeks early on)
A frame that cannot be proved wrong is not a frame; it must be testable
BB-01.1.scgExample: A packaging business manager is told by her sponsor to "do something about e-commerce boxes". In the framing conversation she narrows it to: mid-size Thai online sellers shipping 500-2,000 parcels a month lose about THB 18 per damaged return, with a 3.2% damage rate on current standard cartons. Success is defined as a carton spec that cuts damage below 1.5% at no more than THB 1.20 extra per unit, tested with 5 sellers in 8 weeks. Out of scope: anything requiring new converting equipment at Rayong before FY27.
BB-01.1.practiceTask: Pick one idea currently sitting in your function's pipeline. Write a one-page problem frame using the five parts (who, cost of pain, why now, success measure, out of scope), and mark every number as F (fact, with source) or A (assumption). Book a 30-minute slot with the sponsor and get written confirmation or correction. Output: the signed-off one-pager plus a list of the top three assumptions to test.
commonMistakes: Writing the solution into the problem statement, which closes off cheaper options before evidence exists
Accepting a vague success measure like "grow the segment" instead of a number and a date
Treating sponsor enthusiasm in the room as agreement, without written playback
Listing 12 assumptions with no priority, so the team tests the easy ones first instead of the riskiest

quickCheck.question: Which of these is a properly framed problem?
options: We should launch a subscription service for contractors
Small contractors reorder cement 2-3 times a week and spend ~40 minutes per order by phone; target is under 10 minutes by Q3
Contractors are unhappy with ordering
Our competitor has a digital ordering platform
quickCheck.why: It names the customer, quantifies the pain, and states a measurable target with a date. The others are solutions, vague complaints or competitor observations.

quickCheck.question: What should you ask a sponsor that teams most often skip?
options: What budget do you have?
What decision will you make with the evidence we bring back, and when?
Who else supports this?
Do you like the idea?
quickCheck.why: Tying framing to a specific gate decision keeps the work proportionate and stops open-ended exploration.

quickCheck.question: An assumption in the frame should be treated how?
options: Removed to keep the page clean
Labelled as an assumption and ranked by how much the concept depends on it
Converted into a fact by senior sign-off
Tested only after the business case is approved
quickCheck.why: Framing makes uncertainty visible and prioritised; sign-off does not turn a guess into evidence.

BB-01.1.coachPrompt: Show me the frame your sponsor signed. Which single assumption, if wrong, kills the concept — and what have you done about it this week?

BB-01.2.summary: This reading walks through filling a business model canvas on a concept you are actually working on, block by block, with the emphasis on how the nine blocks must add up financially and operationally. At SCG a canvas is the bridge between a framed problem and an investment case, and it exposes early whether a concept relies on capabilities the group does not have.
objectives: You can complete all nine canvas blocks for a live concept with evidence ratings
You can identify the two or three blocks that carry the most risk and explain why
You can turn a canvas into a short list of testable assumptions for the next gate
keyPoints: Fill the canvas in this order: customer segment, value proposition, channels, revenue, then cost, resources, activities, partners, relationships — demand before delivery
Each block needs a source: interview, pilot data, internal cost data, or explicitly "assumed"
Value proposition must state the customer's alternative today and why yours is better on a dimension they pay for
Revenue block should name the payer, the pricing mechanism and the buying trigger, not just "product sales"
Cost structure must separate one-off build cost from recurring cost per unit sold; the canvas should reconcile roughly to your unit economics
Key partners at SCG are often internal (a plant, a shared service, a dealer network) — treat internal capacity as a negotiated dependency, not a given
Look for contradictions across blocks: a premium value proposition delivered through a low-touch channel usually fails
Version the canvas with a date; a canvas that has not changed in a month means no learning is happening
BB-01.2.scgExample: A chemicals team canvases a recycled-content compound for automotive interior parts. Segment: two Tier-1 suppliers in Rayong needing 30% recycled content to meet their OEM's 2028 target; value proposition: certified recycled content at a 6% price premium versus virgin, with documentation the OEM audit accepts. Cost structure shows THB 4.2m one-off for certification plus a 9% higher feedstock cost, so the premium only works above 1,200 tonnes a year. The riskiest blocks are key resources (stable supply of clean post-industrial feedstock) and partners (the certifier's timeline), so both were moved to the test list.
BB-01.2.practiceTask: Take one live concept and complete a nine-block canvas in one sitting (about 25 minutes), colour-coding each block green (evidence), amber (partial), red (assumed). Then write the three red items as testable statements with a proposed test and cost. Output: dated canvas plus a three-line test plan you can show your sponsor.
commonMistakes: Filling the canvas with aspirations rather than what is true today, so everything reads green
Leaving the cost structure until last and never reconciling it with the revenue block
Assuming internal plants, IT or dealers will provide capacity for free because they are part of SCG
Treating the canvas as a one-off document for a presentation instead of a working artefact updated after each test

quickCheck.question: Which block should be filled first?
options: Key partners
Customer segment
Cost structure
Key activities
quickCheck.why: Delivery-side blocks only make sense once you know who you are serving and what they value.

quickCheck.question: A canvas where every block is marked green after two weeks of work most likely means:
options: The concept is ready for a gate
Evidence ratings are being applied too generously
The team is high performing
Costs are well understood
quickCheck.why: Early concepts are mostly assumption; all-green signals optimism rather than evidence.

quickCheck.question: How should an internal SCG plant supplying trial volumes appear on the canvas?
options: It doesn't — it's internal
As a key partner with an agreed capacity and transfer cost
As a customer segment
Only in the revenue block
quickCheck.why: Internal dependencies carry real cost and scheduling risk and must be negotiated and priced like any partner.

BB-01.2.coachPrompt: Which block on your canvas changed after last week's customer conversations, and what did that change do to your cost per unit?

FIN-01.1.summary: This 12-minute video covers how to build unit economics — price, variable cost, contribution per unit and the volume needed to cover fixed costs — and how to set a price from customer value rather than cost-plus. At SCG gate decisions fail most often because the unit economics were never separated from the total business case, hiding a product that loses money on every unit sold.
objectives: You can calculate contribution margin per unit and breakeven volume for a concept
You can explain the difference between cost-plus and value-based pricing and when each applies
You can identify which cost items are genuinely variable at the volumes you are proposing
keyPoints: Unit economics = price per unit − variable cost per unit = contribution; fixed cost ÷ contribution = breakeven volume
Classify costs honestly: freight, packaging, raw material and commission are usually variable; plant depreciation and sales salaries are not
Value-based pricing starts from the customer's next best alternative plus the value your offer adds, then checks that cost-plus floor
Always state price net of discounts, rebates and dealer margin — gross list price flatters every case
Test sensitivity on the two or three drivers that move contribution most, usually price, raw material cost and volume
Include cost-to-serve: delivery frequency, credit terms and technical support can quietly erase margin on small customers
Check the breakeven volume against real market and plant capacity; if it needs 40% market share, the price is wrong
Show payback in months alongside margin — sponsors decide on cash timing as much as on percentage
FIN-01.1.scgExample: A cement business proposes a bagged low-carbon product at THB 155 per bag versus THB 142 for standard. Variable cost is THB 118 (clinker substitute, bag, freight) and dealer margin is THB 12, so net contribution is THB 25 per bag versus THB 19 on standard. Fixed incremental cost — silo modification and marketing — is THB 9m, giving a breakeven of 360,000 bags, about 8% of the regional bagged volume, which the team judged achievable in year two.
FIN-01.1.practiceTask: Take one product or service line in your function and build a single-unit P&L: net price after all discounts, each variable cost item with a source, contribution, and breakeven volume against the incremental fixed cost. Then flex price by ±5% and show the effect on breakeven. Output: a one-tab model with assumptions labelled, plus one sentence on which driver matters most.
commonMistakes: Using list price instead of net realised price, overstating contribution by 10-15%
Loading allocated overhead into variable cost, which makes breakeven look impossible and kills good ideas
Ignoring cost-to-serve differences between large dealers and small ones
Pricing at cost-plus when the customer's alternative is far more expensive, leaving value on the table

quickCheck.question: Contribution per unit is:
options: Net price minus total cost including allocated overhead
Net price minus variable cost per unit
Gross list price minus raw material cost
Revenue minus fixed cost
quickCheck.why: Contribution covers only variable cost; fixed costs are recovered through volume × contribution.

quickCheck.question: Breakeven volume of 360,000 bags equals 45% of the regional market. The right response is:
options: Proceed — it is only one assumption
Revisit price, cost or scope because the volume is not credible
Increase the marketing budget
Extend the payback period to 10 years
quickCheck.why: A breakeven requiring implausible share means the economics, not the ambition, need changing.
