quickCheck.question: Which cost is most likely variable for a bagged cement concept?
options: Plant depreciation
Regional sales manager salary
Outbound freight per tonne
Head-office IT allocation
quickCheck.why: Freight scales directly with units shipped; the others do not change with incremental volume.

FIN-01.1.coachPrompt: What is your net realised price per unit after every discount and rebate, and how does it compare with the list price you first quoted me?

FIN-01.2.summary: This reading shows how to build best, base and worst cases inside one model rather than three separate spreadsheets, using a single driver sheet so a sponsor can see exactly what changes between scenarios. At SCG gate committees want to know the downside and the trigger points, and a one-model approach makes the case auditable and fast to update.
objectives: You can structure a model with a separate driver sheet so scenarios are switched, not rebuilt
You can define best and worst cases from evidence-based ranges rather than round percentages
You can state the decision triggers that would move the business from base toward worst case
keyPoints: One model, three scenarios: hard-code nothing in calculations; every driver sits in one input block with a scenario switch
Set ranges from real data — historical price volatility, plant ramp-up records, past launch adoption — not ±20% by habit
Worst case should be plausible and survivable, not catastrophic; test the combination of two or three adverse drivers happening together
Best case must include the cost of success: more working capital, faster capex, extra headcount
Report the same four outputs for each scenario: cumulative cash, payback period, peak funding need and IRR or NPV
Identify the breakpoint value for each driver — the price or volume at which the case stops working — and name the early warning indicator for it
Add a short assumption log with owner and date; gate committees challenge sources more than arithmetic
Keep the model to what a reviewer can follow in 10 minutes; complexity hides errors rather than removing risk
FIN-01.2.scgExample: A shared services team models an outsourced invoice-processing hub. Base case: 480,000 invoices a year at THB 14 processing cost, payback 26 months. Worst case combines a slower migration (18 months instead of 12) with volume at 400,000 and a 6% wage increase, pushing payback to 41 months and peak funding to THB 22m. The team flagged migration slippage beyond month 14 as the early warning trigger, with a pre-agreed decision to pause phase two.
FIN-01.2.practiceTask: Rebuild one existing business case in your function as a single model with a driver sheet and a scenario switch. Justify each best/worst range in one line using historical data. Output: a model producing cumulative cash, payback, peak funding and NPV for all three scenarios, plus a list of driver breakpoints and their early warning indicators.
commonMistakes: Maintaining three separate files that drift apart after the first review round
Building worst case by shaving 10% off revenue while leaving costs and timing untouched
Forgetting that the best case consumes more cash earlier through working capital and capex
Presenting scenarios without breakpoints, so the sponsor cannot see what to monitor after approval

quickCheck.question: The main advantage of one model with a driver sheet is:
options: It produces a higher NPV
Scenarios stay consistent and can be updated in minutes
It avoids the need for assumptions
It removes downside risk
quickCheck.why: A single calculation engine with switchable inputs keeps scenarios comparable and auditable.

quickCheck.question: A credible worst case should:
options: Assume everything fails at once
Combine two or three plausible adverse drivers and show peak funding need
Cut revenue by exactly 20%
Match the base case with a longer timeline only
quickCheck.why: Worst case is a planning tool: plausible combined stress plus the cash it requires.

quickCheck.question: Why include the cost of success in the best case?
options: To make the case look conservative
Because faster growth pulls forward capex and working capital, changing peak funding
Because auditors require it
To offset the worst case
quickCheck.why: Rapid volume growth often worsens cash before it improves it; ignoring this understates the funding request.

FIN-01.2.coachPrompt: In your model, which single driver has the lowest breakpoint, and what indicator will tell you within 30 days that you are heading toward it?

GRN-01.1.summary: This 12-minute video explains how to separate sustainability features from sustainability value the customer will actually pay for, by tracing the benefit to the customer's own cost, risk or regulatory obligation. At SCG many green offers are priced on our cost of greening rather than on the buyer's willingness to pay, which is why premiums get negotiated away.
objectives: You can distinguish a green feature from a quantified customer benefit
You can identify which buyer in the customer organisation carries the sustainability obligation
You can test a green premium with at least two customers before committing to a price
keyPoints: Customers pay for three things: compliance they must meet, cost they can reduce, or risk/reputation they must manage — map your green attribute to one of them
Name the person who feels the pain: a procurement officer rarely pays a premium, a sustainability or compliance lead with a reported target often does
Quantify in the customer's units: kg CO2e per tonne delivered, waste diverted per site per month, water saved per production run
Evidence beats claims — third-party certification or verified data is usually what unlocks premium, not the attribute itself
Test willingness to pay by asking about their current spend on the alternative, not by asking "would you pay more?"
Bundle: green attributes often sell better combined with a hard commercial benefit like lower breakage, faster cure time or reduced disposal cost
If no premium exists, green value may still win volume or preferred-supplier status; decide which outcome you are pricing for
Beware of unverifiable claims; overstated environmental benefit is a legal and reputational risk for SCG
GRN-01.1.scgExample: A packaging team offers a mono-material recyclable film to a Thai food manufacturer. Procurement rejects a THB 3.10/kg premium, but the customer's sustainability lead has a commitment to make 100% of packaging recyclable by 2027 and currently pays THB 480,000 a year in extended producer responsibility fees on multi-layer film. Reframed against that fee plus avoided redesign cost, the manufacturer accepts THB 2.40/kg on two SKUs. The deal was won by changing the buyer and the benefit measure, not the product.
GRN-01.1.practiceTask: Choose one green or efficiency attribute in your portfolio. Write a half-page value map: the attribute, the customer benefit in the customer's own units, the person who owns that benefit, the evidence you can show, and their current cost of the alternative. Then call or email two customers to check the numbers. Output: the value map with two customer quotes or corrections.
commonMistakes: Pricing the premium from our cost of low-carbon production rather than the customer's economics
Pitching to procurement only, where sustainability rarely has a budget line
Using vague claims like "eco-friendly" that cannot be verified or compared
Assuming a premium is the only prize, when volume, contract length or supplier status may be worth more

quickCheck.question: The strongest basis for a green premium is usually:
options: Our higher production cost
A regulatory or reported obligation the customer must meet
A general preference for sustainability
Competitor pricing
quickCheck.why: Obligations create budget; preferences usually do not survive procurement negotiation.

quickCheck.question: Best way to test willingness to pay:
options: Ask "would you pay 5% more for a greener option?"
Ask what they currently spend or risk on the alternative, then compare
Run an internal workshop
Benchmark competitor list prices
quickCheck.why: Stated willingness to pay is unreliable; anchoring on their existing costs produces real numbers.

quickCheck.question: If no customer will pay a premium, the right next step is:
options: Drop the concept
Decide whether volume, contract length or preferred-supplier status is the value being bought
Raise the price to signal quality
Absorb the cost quietly
quickCheck.why: Green value can be commercial without a price premium, but the intended payoff must be chosen deliberately.

GRN-01.1.coachPrompt: Who in your customer's organisation actually owns the sustainability number your offer improves, and have you spoken to them directly?

GRN-01.2.summary: This reading covers how to define, baseline and verify the sustainability outcomes a proposition claims, so the number survives customer audit and internal reporting. At SCG a green proposition without a defensible measurement method cannot be sold into large customers' supply-chain reporting or counted toward group targets.
objectives: You can define a green metric with a boundary, baseline and calculation method
You can choose between primary data, supplier data and published factors, and state the uncertainty
You can build a simple verification and reporting routine a customer would accept
keyPoints: Every claim needs four elements: metric, system boundary, baseline comparison and time period (e.g. kg CO2e per tonne delivered, cradle-to-gate, versus FY25 standard product, per quarter)
Baseline choice drives the headline number — document why that baseline was chosen and keep it fixed for the contract period
Data hierarchy: primary measured data > supplier-specific data > regional published emission factors; state which you used and the margin of error
Avoid double counting: if a recycled input already carries a supplier claim, agree who reports the benefit
Report avoided impact separately from absolute impact; customers' reporting frameworks treat them differently
Build the measurement into operations — meter readings, batch records, delivery data — rather than a separate annual exercise
Agree verification level up front: internal review, customer audit, or third-party assurance; each has different cost and lead time
Plan for restatement: if a factor or method changes, publish the revised figure and the reason rather than silently updating
GRN-01.2.scgExample: A cement business claims a 22% reduction in embodied carbon on a blended product. The metric is kg CO2e per tonne of cement, cradle-to-gate, baseline being the FY25 OPC average of 780 kg, measured quarterly from plant clinker-factor and kiln fuel records. Because the fly ash supplier also claims a benefit, the two agreed in writing that only SCG reports it in the product footprint. A third-party assurance costing THB 850,000 was added when a major infrastructure client required it for their own Scope 3 reporting.
GRN-01.2.practiceTask: Take one sustainability claim your function currently makes. Write a one-page measurement note: metric and unit, system boundary, baseline and why, data sources with quality rating, frequency, owner, and verification level. Flag any double-counting risk. Output: the note plus one gap you will close this quarter.
commonMistakes: Quoting a percentage reduction without stating the baseline, which makes the claim unverifiable
Mixing primary and published-factor data without disclosing it, weakening the number under audit
Double counting a benefit that a supplier or recycler is already reporting
Treating measurement as a marketing task rather than embedding it in plant or logistics records

quickCheck.question: A claim of "30% lower carbon" is incomplete without:
options: A customer testimonial
Baseline, boundary and time period
A competitor comparison
A price premium
quickCheck.why: Without baseline, boundary and period the figure cannot be reproduced or audited.

quickCheck.question: Preferred data source when available:
options: Regional published emission factors
Supplier-specific data
Primary measured data from our own operations
Industry association averages
quickCheck.why: Primary measured data has the lowest uncertainty and is most defensible in customer audits.

quickCheck.question: Your fly ash supplier claims the recycling benefit and so do you. This is:
options: Acceptable if both are transparent
Double counting, which must be resolved in writing before the claim is used
Only a problem for regulated sectors
Resolved automatically by certification
quickCheck.why: The same environmental benefit can only be reported once; allocation must be agreed between parties.

GRN-01.2.coachPrompt: Walk me through how you would reproduce your headline sustainability number from raw plant or delivery records — what would an auditor not be able to find?

AIS-01.1.summary: A 12-minute video showing how to run a two-hour AI-assisted market research sprint: framing the question, prompting for structure, and separating AI output into verified facts, sourced claims and hypotheses. It matters at SCG because BU teams often spend three weeks on market packs that a disciplined sprint can draft in a day, leaving more time for judgement and validation.
objectives: You can write a sprint brief that states the decision, the boundary of the market and the three questions AI must answer
You can prompt an AI tool to produce a structured market view and tag every line as verified, sourced or hypothesis
You can produce a one-page research output with an explicit list of facts that must be checked with a human source before use
keyPoints: Start from the decision, not the topic: 'should we add a 1.5mm corrugated line in Rayong?' beats 'research packaging market'.
Define the boundary explicitly — geography, segment, product spec, time horizon — or AI will average across irrelevant markets.
Use a three-pass pattern: pass 1 structure the question, pass 2 generate the market view, pass 3 attack it ('what would make this wrong?').
Tag every AI output line: V (verified against a document you hold), S (sourced, citation exists and you checked it), H (hypothesis to test).
AI is strongest on structure, frameworks, competitor lists and question generation; weakest on current Thai/ASEAN prices, volumes and local regulation.
Never paste customer names, contract terms, unpublished volumes or cost data into public tools — use the approved internal tool per SCG data rules.
Timebox the sprint (90–120 min) and end with a named human validation step: a dealer call, a plant manager, or a trade association contact.
Keep the prompt log with the output so a reviewer can see how the view was built.
AIS-01.1.scgExample: A Cement–Building Materials commercial manager must recommend whether to push mortar sales into three Mekong border provinces next year. She briefs the AI tool with the decision, the provinces, the product spec and a 12-month horizon, and asks for demand drivers, likely competitors and a list of what she would need to know to be wrong. In 70 minutes she gets a structured view naming construction-permit growth and cross-border logistics cost as the two swing factors, plus 14 claims she tags as hypotheses. She then makes two dealer calls and finds the AI's assumed 8% permit growth is closer to 3%, which changes her recommendation from 'expand in all three' to 'pilot in one'.
AIS-01.1.practiceTask: Pick one real market or sourcing question your team faces this quarter. Spend 20–30 minutes: write a six-line sprint brief (decision, boundary, three questions, horizon), run one AI pass, and convert the output into a half-page table with three columns — claim, V/S/H tag, who can verify it. Expected output: the half-page table plus a named person you will call this week to test the single most decision-critical hypothesis.
commonMistakes: Asking a broad topic question ('tell me about the ASEAN packaging market') and receiving a generic answer that cannot change any decision.
Treating AI-generated figures as data because they look precise — unlabelled numbers are hypotheses until sourced.
Pasting confidential SCG volume, price or customer information into a public AI tool.
Ending the sprint at the AI output instead of at a human validation call, so nothing is actually verified.

quickCheck.question: What should a market research sprint brief start with?
options: A list of competitors to profile
The specific decision the research must support
The AI tool and model version
A literature search of public reports
quickCheck.why: Anchoring on the decision sets the boundary and stops the sprint producing interesting but unusable material.

quickCheck.question: An AI output states 'Thai ready-mix demand grew 6.2% in 2024' with no citation you can open. How should you tag it?
options: Verified — the number is specific
Sourced — AI implies it has a source
Hypothesis — to be checked against an industry figure
Discard it immediately
quickCheck.why: Specificity is not evidence. Without a source you can open, it is a hypothesis you carry forward and test.

quickCheck.question: Which task is AI usually weakest at in an SCG market sprint?
options: Generating a competitor framework
Listing questions you have not asked
Current local prices and provincial regulation
Structuring an unstructured problem
quickCheck.why: Fast-moving local prices and regulation are where models are stale or wrong; these need human or documented sources.

AIS-01.1.coachPrompt: Show me the last sprint output you produced — which claim did you tag as a hypothesis, who did you call to test it, and did the answer change your recommendation?

AIS-01.2.summary: An 18-minute reading on building two to four decision-relevant scenarios and using AI to attack a strategy you already favour. It matters because SCG plans often rest on one base case for energy cost, export demand or carbon regulation, and a single-point plan breaks when the assumption moves.
objectives: You can identify the two uncertainties that most affect a specific strategic option and build a 2x2 of scenarios from them
You can use AI as a structured challenger to surface failure modes and disconfirming evidence for your preferred option
You can state, for each scenario, the leading indicator you would watch and the action you would take
keyPoints: Scenarios are not forecasts. Their job is to reveal which choices are robust across futures and which depend on one assumption holding.
Select axes by impact and uncertainty: high impact plus high uncertainty. Things you are confident about belong in the base assumptions, not the axes.
Two axes gives four scenarios; three or four named scenarios is the practical limit for a management discussion.
Name scenarios in plain language that describe the world ('Cheap gas, weak exports'), not labels like 'Scenario B'.
Use AI in the challenger role: 'Argue the opposite case', 'What has to be true for this to fail in 18 months?', 'What evidence would change your mind?'
Convert each scenario to a leading indicator with a threshold and a named owner — e.g. 'if coal delivered cost exceeds X for two consecutive months, revisit'.
Look for the no-regret moves that appear in three or four scenarios; fund these first and stage the rest behind triggers.
Record the assumption set. Most strategy failures are traceable to an assumption nobody wrote down.
AIS-01.2.scgExample: A Chemicals planning team is weighing a debottlenecking investment. They pick two axes: naphtha feedstock spread (wide vs narrow) and China polyolefin export pressure (high vs low), producing four worlds. Using AI as a challenger, they discover their base plan is profitable in three scenarios but loses money whenever narrow spreads and high Chinese export pressure occur together — roughly a 25% chance in their own judgement. They split the investment into a 400 MB no-regret utilities upgrade now and stage the remaining 1,100 MB behind a trigger: two consecutive quarters of spread above the threshold, owned by the planning head.
AIS-01.2.practiceTask: Take one plan or proposal you own. In 20–30 minutes, list your five biggest assumptions, score each on impact and uncertainty, pick the top two as axes, and sketch four scenarios in one line each. Then run one AI prompt asking it to argue why your plan fails in the worst quadrant. Expected output: a one-page 2x2 with a leading indicator and threshold for each scenario, plus one no-regret action you can start now.
commonMistakes: Building optimistic, base and pessimistic cases — these are one variable moved three ways, not scenarios, and they hide the interaction that actually kills the plan.
Choosing axes that are high impact but low uncertainty, which produces four versions of the same future.
Leaving scenarios as narratives with no indicator, threshold or owner, so nobody notices when the world shifts.
Using AI only to write up the scenarios rather than to attack the preferred option.

quickCheck.question: What makes a good scenario axis?
options: High impact and high uncertainty
High impact and high confidence
Easy to measure monthly
Agreed by all stakeholders
quickCheck.why: Low-uncertainty variables belong in base assumptions; axes must be things that could plausibly break the plan.

quickCheck.question: What is the most useful AI prompt when stress-testing a favoured option?
options: Summarise the strategy in one page
Make the case that this plan fails within 18 months and state what would have to be true
List the benefits of the plan
Rewrite the plan for the executive committee
quickCheck.why: AI adds most value as a disciplined challenger that forces disconfirming evidence into view.

quickCheck.question: A scenario set is complete when...
options: Each scenario has a memorable name
There are exactly four of them
Each has a leading indicator, threshold and owner
The CEO has approved the base case
quickCheck.why: Without indicators and owners, scenarios never influence a real decision.

AIS-01.2.coachPrompt: Which assumption in your current plan would hurt you most if it moved, and what indicator and threshold have you set to catch it early?

EXP-01.1.summary: A 12-minute video on writing a one-page executive pre-read that lets the committee decide before the meeting starts. It matters because SCG management committee slots are short, and proposals that arrive without a clear ask, evidence and risk view get deferred rather than rejected.
objectives: You can write a one-page pre-read with a single explicit ask, three supporting evidence points and the top risks with mitigations
You can state the decision needed, the deadline and the cost of delay in the first three lines
You can distinguish material an executive needs to decide from background that belongs in an annex
keyPoints: Lead with the ask: what you want approved, how much, by when. If the reader cannot find this in ten seconds, the page has failed.
Use the A-E-R-N spine: Ask, Evidence (three points maximum), Risks with mitigations, Next step if approved.
Quantify the cost of delay. 'Each month of delay costs 3 MB of avoided freight' converts a discussion into a decision.
State your recommendation among the options considered, and say briefly why the rejected options lost.
Name the risks yourself. Executives trust proposals that surface their own weaknesses more than ones that hide them.
One page, annexes behind. Detail is not removed, it is relocated and referenced.
Write numbers with their source and date so the committee is not arguing about the data instead of the decision.
Send the pre-read at least 48 hours ahead and follow with a two-line message confirming the specific decision required.
EXP-01.1.scgExample: A packaging operations manager wants 18 MB to install automatic strapping on two converting lines. Her pre-read opens: 'Ask: approve 18 MB capex, decision needed by 30 April to hit the September shutdown window.' Evidence is three lines — 1.9 MB annual labour and rework saving per line, payback 4.7 years, two recent hand-strapping injuries. Risks are listed as vendor lead time of 22 weeks with a mitigation of a deposit-secured slot, and she notes delay to the next shutdown pushes benefits out 12 months at a cost of 3.8 MB. The committee approves in six minutes.
EXP-01.1.practiceTask: Take a request you need to make in the next month. Spend 20–30 minutes drafting a one-page pre-read using the A-E-R-N spine, with every number carrying a source and date, and everything else moved to an annex list. Expected output: one page where a colleague who knows nothing about the topic can tell you, within 15 seconds of reading, what you are asking for and by when.
commonMistakes: Building context and background for half a page before the ask appears.
Offering five options with no recommendation, which pushes the analytical work onto the committee.
Hiding risks, which forces the committee to find them and destroys confidence in the rest of the paper.
Using numbers without source or date, so the meeting becomes a debate about data quality.

quickCheck.question: Where should the ask appear in an executive pre-read?
options: In the conclusion after the evidence
In the first three lines
In the annex with the financials
In the covering email only
quickCheck.why: Executives read for the decision first; burying the ask guarantees the paper is skimmed and deferred.

quickCheck.question: Why include the cost of delay?
options: It fills the page
It converts an open discussion into a dated decision
It is a regulatory requirement
It replaces the risk section
quickCheck.why: Quantified delay cost gives the committee a reason to decide now rather than defer.

quickCheck.question: You have 12 pages of supporting analysis. What do you do?
options: Include all of it so nothing is missed
Cut the analysis down to what fits
Keep one page and reference the analysis as a numbered annex
Present it verbally instead
quickCheck.why: Detail is relocated, not deleted — the one page carries the decision, the annex carries the proof.

EXP-01.1.coachPrompt: Hand me your latest pre-read. Can I find the ask, the deadline and the top risk in under 20 seconds without you explaining anything?

EXP-01.2.summary: An 18-minute reading on structuring and rehearsing a six-minute recorded executive pitch, including handling the questions that follow. It matters because SCG increasingly uses recorded pitches for gate reviews and cross-BU funding, where you get one take and no room to recover from a slow start.
objectives: You can structure a six-minute pitch into a 60-second ask, three minutes of evidence, a risk section and a close that states the next step
You can rehearse against the clock and cut to the time limit without losing the ask or the risk
You can prepare short, direct answers to the three questions an executive audience is most likely to ask
keyPoints: Budget the six minutes: 60s ask and why now, 3 min evidence, 90s risks and mitigations, 30s next step and decision date.
Open with the sentence you want repeated in the executive's own summary of your case — one sentence, no preamble.
Three evidence points only, each with a number, a source and a date. A fourth point dilutes rather than strengthens.
Say the risks aloud. Recorded pitches that skip risk invite a long written challenge afterwards.
Rehearse twice against a timer and cut 20%. Almost every first draft runs eight to nine minutes.
Speak at a steady pace with pauses after each number; rushing signals low confidence more than any word choice.
Prepare a 30-second answer for the three predictable questions: why now, what if the assumptions are wrong, and who else must agree.
Close with a specific next step and a date, not 'happy to discuss'.
EXP-01.2.scgExample: A shared-services manager records a six-minute pitch to consolidate three regional invoice-processing teams into one hub. He opens: 'I am asking to approve a nine-month consolidation that saves 24 MB a year from FY27 and cuts invoice cycle time from 6.2 to 3.5 days.' His three evidence points are a time-and-motion study from March, a pilot in the Northern region showing 31% fewer touches, and benchmark data. He spends 90 seconds on the two real risks — 14 affected staff and a two-month transition dip — with the redeployment plan and the parallel-run mitigation. He closes asking for a decision by 15 June so the hub opens before the fiscal year close; the committee approves with one condition.
EXP-01.2.practiceTask: Record a six-minute pitch on a real proposal using your phone, without slides. Then watch it with a timer and mark where the ask appears, how long the evidence runs and whether risks were stated. Expected output: a revised second recording within six minutes where the ask lands in the first 20 seconds and at least one risk is named with a mitigation, plus three written 30-second answers to the questions you expect.
commonMistakes: Spending two minutes on background and context, leaving no time for risks or the close.
Reading slides or a script aloud, which flattens delivery and pushes the recording over time.
Ending with 'happy to answer questions' instead of a named next step and a decision date.
Not rehearsing against a clock, then rushing the last two minutes and losing the ask entirely.

quickCheck.question: In a six-minute pitch, roughly how long should the ask and 'why now' take?
options: About 60 seconds at the start
Two to three minutes
30 seconds at the end
As long as the evidence section
quickCheck.why: A tight 60-second opening ask frames everything that follows and survives even if the listener stops early.

quickCheck.question: How many evidence points should a six-minute pitch carry?
options: One, repeated
Three, each with number, source and date
Five to six for completeness
As many as the data allows
quickCheck.why: Three well-sourced points are memorable; more dilutes the argument and eats the risk section.

quickCheck.question: What is the strongest way to handle risk in a recorded pitch?
options: Omit it and wait for questions
Mention risks exist but stay general
Name the top risks with specific mitigations
Put risks only in the written annex
quickCheck.why: Naming risks with mitigations builds credibility and pre-empts a long written challenge after the recording.

EXP-01.2.coachPrompt: Play me the first 30 seconds of your recorded pitch — what exactly are you asking for, and by when?

LTC-01.1.summary: A 12-minute video on standing up a cross-BU team in the first two weeks: clarifying the mandate, decision rights, gate criteria and working rhythm. It matters because SCG cross-BU work mixes people with different bosses, incentives and BU calendars, and unclear decision rights is the most common reason these teams stall.
objectives: You can write a one-page team charter covering mandate, scope boundary, decision rights and gate dates
You can agree each member's time commitment in writing with their home-BU line manager
You can set a meeting and escalation rhythm that fits the gate schedule rather than the calendar
keyPoints: Write the mandate as one sentence including what is out of scope. Cross-BU teams drift because nobody drew the boundary.
Separate three decision rights explicitly: who decides, who must be consulted, who is only informed. Ambiguity here costs weeks.
Secure time in writing from each member's line manager — 'two days a week until the June gate' beats a verbal yes.
State the gate criteria on day one. The team should know what evidence will be judged and by whom before it starts work.
Name a single accountable sponsor. Two sponsors from two BUs with equal authority produces deadlock.
Set the rhythm to the gate: weekly 30-minute working checkpoint, fortnightly sponsor update, escalation path with a 48-hour response commitment.
Surface the incentive conflicts in week one — if one BU's KPI improves and the other's worsens, say it out loud and get the sponsor to rule.
Agree how you will handle disagreement before you have one: escalate with both positions written, not by email argument.
LTC-01.1.scgExample: A cross-BU team from Cement, Packaging and Logistics is formed to pilot shared regional warehousing. In week one the lead writes a one-page charter: mandate is a six-month pilot in two provinces, out of scope is any change to BU pricing. She secures written commitments — two days a week from Logistics, one day from each of the other two — and gets the CFO named as single sponsor. She also flags on day three that the pilot moves 4 MB of cost from Packaging onto Cement's P&L; the sponsor rules that the pilot is measured on combined cost, avoiding a dispute that would have surfaced at the gate. The team reaches its first gate two weeks early.
LTC-01.1.practiceTask: Take a cross-functional or cross-BU initiative you are involved in. Spend 20–30 minutes drafting a one-page charter: mandate sentence with an explicit out-of-scope line, a decide/consult/inform table naming individuals, gate dates with criteria, and each member's committed days per week. Expected output: the charter plus a list of the two commitments or decision rights that are currently unconfirmed and who you will ask this week.
commonMistakes: Starting the work before decision rights are agreed, then discovering at the gate that a BU never accepted the outcome.
Accepting verbal time commitments that evaporate when the member's home BU hits a busy period.
Appointing co-sponsors from two BUs, which turns every contested call into a negotiation.
Hiding the incentive conflict between BUs to keep the early meetings harmonious.

quickCheck.question: What is the most common cause of cross-BU teams stalling?
options: Insufficient budget
Unclear decision rights
Poor meeting facilities
Too few team members
quickCheck.why: When it is unclear who decides and who is merely consulted, contested calls loop back through BUs and weeks are lost.

quickCheck.question: A member's line manager gives a verbal 'yes, he can help'. What should you do?
options: Proceed — the verbal yes is enough
Confirm specific days per week in writing until the next gate
Ask the sponsor to reassign the member full time
Reduce the scope to fit the uncertainty
quickCheck.why: Written, time-bound commitments survive the home BU's busy periods; vague goodwill does not.

quickCheck.question: When should gate criteria be agreed?
options: At the gate itself
Halfway through, when evidence is clearer
On day one, before work starts
After the first sponsor update
quickCheck.why: Knowing what evidence will be judged, and by whom, directs the team's effort from the first week.

LTC-01.1.coachPrompt: For your current cross-BU team, name the single person who decides at the next gate — and tell me how you know the other BUs accept that.

LTC-01.2.summary: An 18-minute reading on leading a mixed team through a pivot or a stop decision: communicating the outcome, protecting people's standing, and capturing what was learned. It matters because SCG's gated way of working produces stops by design, and how a leader handles them determines whether good people volunteer for the next cross-BU assignment.
objectives: You can deliver a pivot or stop message that states the decision, the reason and what happens to each person within 48 hours of the gate
You can run a short learning review that produces reusable findings rather than blame
You can place team members and close down commitments so the stop is clean
keyPoints: Communicate within 48 hours. The gap between the gate and the message is filled by rumour, and rumour is always worse than the facts.
Lead with the decision and the reason, in that order: 'The gate decision is to stop. Demand at the tested price was 40% below the threshold.'
Separate the decision from the people. A stop means the evidence answered the question — that is the gate working, not a failure of the team.
Answer the three questions everyone has: what happens to me, when do I know, and who do I report to next.
Distinguish a pivot from a stop in writing. Pivots keep the mandate but change the approach; teams that are told 'pivot' while the budget is being removed lose trust fast.
Run the learning review within a week while memory is accurate: what did we assume, what did the evidence show, what would we test earlier next time.
Write the findings to be reusable by other BUs — a stop that produces a validated 'this does not work at this price' is a real asset.
Close down cleanly: cancel commitments, release vendor slots, return data and equipment, and write each member's contribution to their line manager.
LTC-01.2.scgExample: A cross-BU team piloting a low-carbon mortar for the retail dealer channel is stopped at the second gate after dealer uptake reaches 11% against a 30% threshold. The lead calls the team within 24 hours, states the decision and the number, and confirms that all six members return to their home BUs by month-end with a written contribution note to each line manager. The learning review five days later finds the assumption that dealers would carry two SKUs was never tested, and recommends a two-week dealer shelf-space test as a gate-one requirement for future channel pilots. Two members are recruited onto the next pilot, partly because the stop was handled cleanly.
LTC-01.2.practiceTask: Take a real or imminent pivot or stop in your area. Spend 20–30 minutes writing the announcement message — decision, reason with the number, what happens to each person and by when — and a five-line learning review template with the three questions filled in from your own assumptions. Expected output: the draft message reviewed by your sponsor, plus one reusable finding written in a form another BU could apply.
commonMistakes: Delaying the message while placements are finalised, so the team hears second-hand and assumes the worst.
Softening a stop into 'we are pausing' when the budget and people are gone, which damages credibility for the next assignment.
Running the learning review as a search for who was wrong rather than which assumption was untested.
Skipping the clean close-down — leaving vendor commitments, data and equipment unresolved for someone else to find months later.

quickCheck.question: How quickly should a gate stop be communicated to the team?
options: Within 48 hours
Once all redeployments are confirmed
At the next scheduled team meeting
After the sponsor writes the formal report
quickCheck.why: Delay is filled by rumour; state the decision and reason first, and give a date for placement answers.

quickCheck.question: What distinguishes a pivot from a stop?
options: A pivot has a smaller budget
A pivot keeps the mandate but changes the approach; a stop ends the mandate
A pivot is announced verbally, a stop in writing
There is no practical difference
quickCheck.why: Labelling a stop as a pivot to soften it misleads the team and destroys trust at the next gate.

quickCheck.question: What is the main output of a post-stop learning review?
options: An account of who made the wrong call
A reusable finding about which assumption failed and what to test earlier
A revised business case for a second attempt
A record for the performance appraisal file
quickCheck.why: The value of a stop is the validated knowledge it hands to the next team; blame produces nothing reusable.

LTC-01.2.coachPrompt: Think of the last pivot or stop you led or witnessed — how long was the gap between the gate decision and the team hearing it directly from you, and what did people hear in between?
